title: Acute Appendicitis
source_title: WSES Jerusalem guidelines: acute appendicitis

redFlags: Generalized peritonitis
Hemodynamic instability or sepsis
Rigid abdomen
Rapidly worsening pain or systemic illness
Pregnancy/immunosuppression with concerning symptoms
symptoms: Abdominal pain possibly migrating to right lower quadrant
Loss of appetite
Nausea or vomiting
Fever
Pain worsened by movement or cough
physicalSigns: Right lower quadrant tenderness
Localized guarding
Pain with movement or cough
Possible fever and tachycardia
Variable findings in pregnancy, older adults, and children

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Possible pregnancy, pelvic pain, vaginal bleeding, or instability.
Acute unilateral pelvic pain with supportive adnexal imaging.
Colicky flank-to-groin pain and possible hematuria.
Diarrhea or diffuse symptoms may predominate; serial examination helps distinguish.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Serial focused abdominal examination — Appendicitis or peritoneal irritation
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Persistent or evolving focal tenderness, guarding, or movement pain.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Clinical course and serial findings support diagnosis.

ruleIn.testName: Ultrasound or CT selected by age, pregnancy, and local protocol
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Ultrasound or CT selected by age, pregnancy, and local protocol — Appendicitis
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Imaging consistent with inflamed appendix or complication.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Clarifies uncertain presentations and identifies complications.

ruleOut.testName: Urinalysis
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Urinalysis — Urinary infection or calculus
ruleOut.expectedFinding: No findings sufficient to explain symptoms when urinary disease is unlikely.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Urinary infection or calculus
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Assesses common mimics but does not independently exclude appendicitis.

ruleOut.testName: Pregnancy test when relevant
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Pregnancy test when relevant — Pregnancy-related abdominal pain

ruleOut.targetCondition: Pregnancy-related abdominal pain
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Informs differential, imaging, and gynecologic urgency.

title: Acute Coronary Syndrome
source_title: NICE NG185: Acute coronary syndromes

redFlags: Persistent or recurrent ischemic pain
High-risk ECG changes
Hemodynamic instability
Pulmonary edema or cardiogenic shock
Cardiac arrest or malignant arrhythmia
symptoms: Chest pressure, tightness, heaviness, or pain
Discomfort to arm, jaw, back, neck, or upper abdomen
Shortness of breath
Nausea, vomiting, or sweating
Fatigue, lightheadedness, or syncope
physicalSigns: Diaphoresis or pallor
Tachycardia, bradycardia, or arrhythmia
Hypotension or hypertension
Signs of acute heart failure
Examination may be normal

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Abrupt severe pain, pulse/BP asymmetry, neurologic deficit, or aortic regurgitation.
Pleuritic pain, unexplained hypoxemia/tachycardia, and VTE risk.
Often positional or pleuritic pain with characteristic ECG changes.
Meal-related, positional, or reproducible features do not alone exclude ACS.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: 12-lead ECG repeated when symptoms persist/evolve — ACS
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Possible ST elevation, ischemic ST depression, T-wave inversion, or dynamic changes.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Rapid interpretation guides reperfusion and risk management.

ruleIn.testName: Serial high-sensitivity troponin using local pathway
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Serial high-sensitivity troponin using local pathway — Acute myocardial injury
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Rise/fall with a value above assay threshold in clinical context.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Supports diagnosis and risk assessment with symptoms and ECG.

ruleOut.testName: Serial ECG and troponin pathway
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Serial ECG and troponin pathway — Acute MI
ruleOut.expectedFinding: No evolving ischemic ECG or significant troponin change by validated pathway.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Acute MI
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: A single normal ECG or early troponin does not exclude ACS.

ruleOut.testName: Chest radiograph when indicated
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Chest radiograph when indicated — Alternative thoracic cause or complication
ruleOut.expectedFinding: No evident pneumothorax, major edema, or other thoracic cause.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Alternative thoracic cause or complication
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Assesses selected mimics but does not rule out ACS.

actions: Administer indicated antiplatelet and other therapies per current Saudi/local protocol after checking contraindications and bleeding risk.
Give oxygen only when indicated by hypoxemia or respiratory distress.
Assess for alternative life-threatening diagnoses before potentially harmful therapies.
Admit or transfer for cardiology-led risk assessment and treatment.
Review ECG, serial troponin, renal function, bleeding risk, and comorbidities.

title: Acute Coronary Syndrome
source_title: 2025 ACC/AHA/ACEP/NAEMSP/SCAI ACS Guideline

redFlags: Persistent or recurrent ischemic pain
High-risk ECG changes
Hemodynamic instability
Pulmonary edema or cardiogenic shock
Cardiac arrest or malignant arrhythmia
symptoms: Chest pressure, tightness, heaviness, or pain
Discomfort to arm, jaw, back, neck, or upper abdomen
Shortness of breath
Nausea, vomiting, or sweating
Fatigue, lightheadedness, or syncope
physicalSigns: Diaphoresis or pallor
Tachycardia, bradycardia, or arrhythmia
Hypotension or hypertension
Signs of acute heart failure
Examination may be normal

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Abrupt severe pain, pulse/BP asymmetry, neurologic deficit, or aortic regurgitation.
Pleuritic pain, unexplained hypoxemia/tachycardia, and VTE risk.
Often positional or pleuritic pain with characteristic ECG changes.
Meal-related, positional, or reproducible features do not alone exclude ACS.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: 12-Lead ECG — Acute coronary syndrome
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Look for ST elevation, ischemic ST depression, or T-wave inversion.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Must be acquired and interpreted within 10 minutes of arrival. Do not rely on a single normal ECG to rule out ACS.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: High-Sensitivity Troponin (hs-cTn) — Acute myocardial injury
ruleIn.expectedFinding: A rise or fall above the assay threshold supports the diagnosis.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Draw at presentation (Hour 0) and repeat at 1 or 2 hours depending on the validated assay pathway.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Basic Metabolic Panel & CBC — Renal function, electrolyte abnormalities and bleeding risk
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Baseline renal function, electrolytes, and hemoglobin.
ruleIn.targetCondition: Renal function, electrolyte abnormalities and bleeding risk
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Assess baseline renal function (crucial for anticoagulant dosing), electrolytes, and baseline hemoglobin to evaluate bleeding risk before initiating aggressive antiplatelet therapy.

ruleOut.testName: Chest Radiograph (Portable)
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Chest Radiograph (Portable) — Alternative thoracic causes
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Assess for mimics like pneumothorax or signs suggesting aortic dissection.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Alternative thoracic causes
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: User-supplied directive: Perform within 30 minutes to rule out mimics like pneumothorax or aortic dissection, but note that it does not rule out ACS. Clinical review flag: a chest radiograph cannot reliably exclude aortic dissection; the 30-minute target requires local validation.

pathophysiology.summary:
Acute coronary syndrome (ACS) describes an acute spectrum of myocardial ischaemia caused by an abrupt imbalance between oxygen supply and myocardial demand. A common initiating event is disruption or erosion of an atherosclerotic coronary plaque. Exposure of thrombogenic material activates platelets and the coagulation cascade, producing a thrombus that may partially or completely obstruct coronary flow. Vasoconstriction, distal microembolisation, and pre-existing fixed stenoses can further reduce perfusion. Less commonly, coronary spasm, spontaneous dissection, embolism, or severe supply–demand mismatch produces an ACS-like presentation without acute plaque thrombosis.

The amount and duration of flow reduction, collateral circulation, and myocardial oxygen demand determine whether injury remains transient or progresses to irreversible necrosis. Ischaemic myocardium develops electrical instability and impaired contractility; this can cause dynamic ECG changes, ventricular dysfunction, acute heart failure, shock, or malignant arrhythmia. When cardiomyocyte injury occurs, intracellular proteins including cardiac troponin enter the circulation. A rise or fall in troponin indicates acute myocardial injury, but infarction requires interpretation alongside evidence of ischaemia such as symptoms, ECG findings, imaging, or coronary thrombus. Therefore, ACS is not defined by a single symptom, ECG, or biomarker result. The clinical spectrum includes unstable angina and myocardial infarction with or without persistent ST elevation; the pattern reflects the severity and persistence of ischaemia and the presence of myocardial necrosis. Older adults, women, and people with diabetes may have less typical symptoms, so assessment integrates the history, serial ECGs, assay-specific troponin pathways, haemodynamic state, and competing time-critical diagnoses. This explanation is an educational synthesis; classification and treatment decisions must follow current local protocols and specialist assessment.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Focal consolidation on chest X-ray, significant fever, and localized crackles rather than generalized wheeze.
Bilateral basal crackles, elevated JVP, cardiomegaly or pleural effusions on X-ray, and elevated BNP.
Consider if dyspnea onset is sudden and pleuritic, with an absence of increased sputum purulence, accompanied by tachycardia or right heart strain on ECG.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Hypercapnic Respiratory Failure
ruleIn.expectedFinding: pH < 7.35 with PaCO2 > 45 mmHg mandates immediate BiPAP initiation.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Mandatory if SpO2 < 92% or signs of fatigue to assess need for non-invasive ventilation (NIV).

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Arrhythmia & Ischemia
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Assess for atrial fibrillation, multifocal atrial tachycardia, or acute ischemia.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Identify cardiac precipitants or complications of hypoxia/medications.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Pathogen Identification
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Only indicated if sputum is purulent or if the patient fails initial empiric antibiotics.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Direct antimicrobial therapy in refractory cases.

ruleOut.modalityTarget: Complications & Alternatives
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Look for pneumothorax, focal infiltrates (pneumonia), or pulmonary edema.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Complications & Alternatives
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Exclude alternative causes of acute dyspnea.

pathophysiology.summary: Airway inflammation and mucus increase expiratory flow limitation and dynamic hyperinflation; infection or pollutants can worsen ventilation-perfusion mismatch. Severe episodes may cause hypercapnia, fatigue, and respiratory muscle failure. This topic is educational and should be interpreted alongside current local pathways and patient-specific assessment.
keyMechanisms: Airway inflammation and mucus increase expiratory flow limitation and dynamic hyperinflation
infection or pollutants can worsen ventilation-perfusion mismatch. Severe episodes may cause hypercapnia, fatigue, and respiratory muscle failure.

clinicalManagement.title: Step 1: Oxygenation Target
actions: Administer controlled oxygen via Venturi mask.
Strict Target: SpO2 88–92%. Do not over-oxygenate due to the risk of worsening V/Q mismatch and hypercapnia.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Immediate

clinicalManagement.title: Step 2: Pharmacological Interventions
actions: Bronchodilators: Salbutamol 2.5–5 mg nebulized + Ipratropium 500 mcg nebulized every 1–4 hours as needed.
Systemic Corticosteroids: Prednisolone 40 mg PO daily for 5 days. (Use IV Hydrocortisone only if patient is unable to take oral medication).

Antibiotics: Indicated ONLY if all 3 cardinal symptoms are present, OR if 2 are present (one being increased purulence), OR if requiring mechanical ventilation. Give Azithromycin or Doxycycline for 5–7 days.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Start promptly and reassess

clinicalManagement.title: Step 3: Ventilatory Support Branch
actions: If patient improves: Transition to standard maintenance inhalers and monitor SpO2.
If respiratory acidosis persists (pH < 7.35): Initiate Non-Invasive Ventilation (BiPAP).
Transition to standard maintenance inhalers and monitor SpO2.

title: Acute Ischemic Stroke
source_title: NICE NG128: Stroke and TIA in over 16s

redFlags: New disabling focal neurologic deficit
Reduced consciousness or airway compromise
Severe sudden headache or vomiting
Seizure at onset or worsening deficit
Unknown last-known-well time
symptoms: Sudden unilateral face/arm/leg weakness or numbness
Sudden speech or language difficulty
Sudden visual loss or diplopia
Sudden imbalance or incoordination
Sudden focal deficit
physicalSigns: Facial asymmetry
Unilateral weakness or sensory loss
Aphasia or dysarthria
Visual field deficit or gaze deviation
Ataxia or neglect

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: May present similarly; urgent imaging is required before reperfusion decisions.
Can mimic focal deficit and should be checked immediately.
Seizure or postictal state may be present, but stroke can also provoke seizure.
May cause evolving positive symptoms; new deficits require urgent stroke assessment.

ruleIn.testName: Urgent noncontrast CT and vascular imaging when indicated
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Urgent noncontrast CT and vascular imaging when indicated — Ischemic stroke/large-vessel occlusion
ruleIn.expectedFinding: CT may initially be normal or show ischemic change; vascular imaging may identify occlusion.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Excludes hemorrhage and supports reperfusion/thrombectomy decisions.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Bedside capillary glucose — Hypoglycemia mimic or comorbidity

ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Rapidly identifies a treatable mimic.

ruleOut.expectedFinding: No acute hemorrhage on appropriate initial imaging.

ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Hemorrhage must be assessed before ischemic reperfusion.

ruleOut.expectedFinding: No acute arrhythmia; normal result does not exclude embolic source.

pathophysiology.summary: An acute exacerbation is a sustained worsening of airflow obstruction caused by bronchial smooth-muscle constriction, airway-wall oedema and mucus plugging on a background of variable airway inflammation. Severe obstruction raises the work of breathing, produces ventilation-perfusion mismatch and may progress from hypocapnia to carbon-dioxide retention as respiratory muscles fatigue.
keyMechanisms: Trigger-driven airway inflammation and bronchial hyper-responsiveness narrow conducting airways.
Mucosal oedema and tenacious secretions amplify expiratory flow limitation and dynamic hyperinflation.
Ventilation-perfusion mismatch causes hypoxaemia; a normalising or rising carbon dioxide level in a distressed patient can indicate fatigue.
Prolonged expiration and air trapping increase intrathoracic pressure and the work of breathing.

clinicalManagement.title: Immediate assessment and stabilisation
actions: Use an airway-breathing-circulation approach and call senior emergency support for severe or life-threatening features.
Position upright when tolerated, establish monitoring and obtain intravenous access without delaying inhaled therapy.
Give controlled oxygen to the locally approved saturation target and reassess frequently.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Immediately on arrival

clinicalManagement.title: Reverse bronchoconstriction
actions: Give repeated inhaled short-acting beta-2 agonist using an appropriate delivery system.
Add inhaled ipratropium bromide in severe or life-threatening exacerbation.
Document response using symptoms, respiratory effort, oxygenation and peak flow where feasible.
Escalate immediately to a senior emergency/critical-care clinician.
Consider continuous nebulised bronchodilator delivery and intravenous magnesium sulfate under the approved local protocol.

actions: Administer systemic corticosteroid promptly unless contraindicated.
Review likely trigger, adherence and recent corticosteroid exposure.
Do not use antibiotics routinely unless bacterial infection is clinically supported.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Early in the first hour

clinicalManagement.title: Structured reassessment
actions: Repeat respiratory rate, work of breathing, speech, oxygen saturation and peak flow where possible.
Check for complications and alternative diagnoses if the trajectory is not improving.
Escalate for ventilatory support planning before exhaustion or reduced consciousness develops.

clinicalManagement.title: Determine safe disposition
actions: Admit patients with persistent severe features, oxygen requirement, poor social support or high relapse risk.
Before discharge, verify inhaler technique, provide an individualised written action plan and arrange controller therapy review.
Explain explicit emergency return precautions.

pathophysiology.summary: Periodic health examination is a risk-based preventive-care process rather than a disease episode. It identifies modifiable cardiovascular, metabolic, cancer, infectious, mental-health and functional risks before symptoms or irreversible complications develop, while avoiding screening that has an unfavourable balance of benefit and harm.
keyMechanisms: Age, sex, family history, exposures and comorbidity alter baseline disease probability and screening benefit.
Repeated measurement can detect trajectories in blood pressure, adiposity, glycaemia and lipids before complications emerge.
Evidence-based screening shifts selected cancers and chronic diseases toward earlier diagnosis.
Shared decisions reduce harms from false positives, overdiagnosis and preventive medicines with small net benefit.

title: Antenatal Care for Uncomplicated Pregnancy
source_title: Gabbe's Obstetrics: Normal and Problem Pregnancies, 9th edition

Severe headache, visual change, or upper abdominal pain later in pregnancy
Reduced fetal movement after the expected pattern is established
Fever, fluid loss, or preterm contractions

physicalSigns: Record observations and a focused examination directed to the organ system and competing diagnoses in this topic.

Use serial reassessment when the condition or treatment can change over hours or days.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Pain/bleeding and uncertain location require urgent assessment.
Symptoms or ultrasound pattern may suggest abnormal gestation.
Comorbidity or prior complication changes care setting and schedule.

ruleIn.testName: Dating ultrasound and gestation-appropriate fetal screening
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Dating ultrasound and gestation-appropriate fetal screening — Gestational age, fetal number and structural/developmental concerns

ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Sets the pregnancy timetable and offers informed, risk-appropriate screening under the Saudi antenatal pathway.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Full blood count — Anaemia or platelet abnormality
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Low haemoglobin or abnormal platelets require assessment using pregnancy-appropriate reference ranges.

ruleIn.testName: Blood group, RhD and antibody screen

ruleIn.targetCondition: RhD status and clinically significant red-cell antibodies

ruleOut.testName: Infection screening selected by the antenatal pathway
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Infection screening selected by the antenatal pathway — Maternal infection with implications for pregnancy or the newborn

title: Asthma
source_title: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd edition

redFlags: Silent chest or inability to speak during attack
Night waking or reliever use rising rapidly
Prior intensive-care admission or severe attack
Persistent symptoms despite verified treatment and technique
symptoms: Evaluate the characteristic symptom pattern of Asthma, including onset, evolution, severity, associated symptoms, precipitating factors, complications, and relevant negative findings.
Clarify onset, progression, associated symptoms, baseline function, medicines and the patient’s own priorities.
Ask about relevant risk factors and context described in the case; document important negative findings rather than assuming their absence.
physicalSigns: Record observations and a focused examination directed to the organ system and competing diagnoses in this topic.
Assess functional change, comorbidity, hydration/perfusion where relevant, and baseline status.
Use serial reassessment when the condition or treatment can change over hours or days.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Persistent obstruction and exposure history may suggest another or overlapping diagnosis.
Inspiratory symptoms and targeted assessment may clarify.
Assess cardiovascular or acute multisystem allergic features.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Spirometry with bronchodilator response — Variable expiratory airflow limitation
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Obstruction with reversibility supports asthma; normal spirometry between episodes does not exclude it.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Provides objective support for the diagnosis instead of relying on symptoms alone.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Peak-flow diary when indicated — Variability in expiratory airflow
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Variation over time or with exposure supports variable airflow limitation when measurements are reliable.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Helps investigate intermittent or work-related symptoms when office spirometry is inconclusive.

ruleOut.testName: Focused assessment for competing causes of wheeze or dyspnoea
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Focused assessment for competing causes of wheeze or dyspnoea — COPD, cardiac disease, upper-airway dysfunction or another mimic
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Smoking history, fixed obstruction, cardiac signs or upper-airway symptoms direct additional testing.
ruleOut.targetCondition: COPD, cardiac disease, upper-airway dysfunction or another mimic
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Prevents misdiagnosis; select a named additional test only for the suspected alternative.

title: Atrial Fibrillation [Adapted from NICE]
source_title: NICE NG196: Atrial fibrillation — diagnosis and management

redFlags: Haemodynamic instability, shock, ongoing myocardial ischaemia or severe pulmonary oedema
New focal neurological deficit suggesting stroke
Syncope with a very rapid or very slow ventricular response
Acute decompensated heart failure or pre-excited atrial fibrillation
symptoms: Palpitations or an irregular heartbeat
Breathlessness or reduced exercise tolerance
Fatigue, dizziness, presyncope or syncope
Chest discomfort or presentation with stroke or transient ischaemic attack
physicalSigns: Irregularly irregular pulse
Variable first heart sound and pulse deficit
Tachycardia or, with conduction disease or medication, bradycardia
Signs of heart failure, valve disease or systemic embolism

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Organised flutter activity on electrocardiogram, often with a regular or patterned ventricular response.
Discrete premature P waves with intervening sinus rhythm rather than sustained fibrillatory activity.
At least three P-wave morphologies and an isoelectric baseline, often in severe pulmonary disease.
Consistent P waves and a physiological trigger; careful lead review separates artefact from atrial activity.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: 12-lead electrocardiogram — Atrial fibrillation
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Irregularly irregular R-R intervals with no consistent discrete P waves.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Provides rhythm confirmation and identifies conduction, ischaemic or pre-excitation features that alter management.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Ambulatory electrocardiographic monitoring — Paroxysmal atrial fibrillation
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Intermittent electrocardiographically documented atrial fibrillation during symptoms or silent episodes.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Monitoring duration should match symptom frequency when the resting electrocardiogram is normal.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Transthoracic echocardiography when indicated — Structural or functional heart disease
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Atrial enlargement, ventricular dysfunction, valve disease or another finding that changes management.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Supports rhythm-control planning, heart-failure assessment and selected refinement of thromboembolic risk.

ruleOut.testName: Thyroid function testing
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Thyroid function testing — Thyrotoxicosis
ruleOut.expectedFinding: No biochemical hyperthyroidism, or a reversible driver is identified.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Thyrotoxicosis
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Thyroid disease can precipitate atrial fibrillation and requires concurrent treatment.

ruleOut.testName: Electrolytes, renal and liver function
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Electrolytes, renal and liver function — Metabolic precipitant or medicine contraindication
ruleOut.expectedFinding: No correctable electrolyte disturbance; organ function is adequate for the selected medicine or prompts adjustment.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Metabolic precipitant or medicine contraindication
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Identifies reversible contributors and is essential before anticoagulant or antiarrhythmic selection.

ruleOut.testName: Acute coronary and pulmonary assessment when clinically indicated
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Acute coronary and pulmonary assessment when clinically indicated — Acute coronary syndrome or pulmonary embolism
ruleOut.expectedFinding: No acute ischaemic or thromboembolic trigger, or one is identified and treated through its urgent pathway.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Acute coronary syndrome or pulmonary embolism
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: New atrial fibrillation may be secondary to another time-critical condition.

pathophysiology.summary: Atrial fibrillation is a supraventricular tachyarrhythmia with disorganised atrial activation and ineffective atrial contraction. Irregular ventricular conduction can cause symptoms or tachycardia-mediated dysfunction, while atrial blood stasis promotes thrombus formation and systemic embolism.
keyMechanisms: Ectopic atrial triggers and a susceptible atrial substrate sustain chaotic electrical activation.
Loss of coordinated atrial contraction and irregular atrioventricular conduction reduce haemodynamic efficiency.
Blood stasis, endothelial dysfunction and prothrombotic factors increase left-atrial thrombus and stroke risk.
Hypertension, heart failure, valve disease, thyroid disease, obesity, sleep apnoea and alcohol can promote onset or recurrence.

clinicalManagement.title: Assess stability and reversible triggers
actions: Assess airway, breathing, circulation, ischaemia, heart failure and neurological status.
Obtain a 12-lead electrocardiogram and correct hypoxia, electrolyte disturbance or another precipitant.
Seek senior cardiology/critical-care support for unstable or pre-excited atrial fibrillation.
Perform urgent synchronised electrical cardioversion under the locally approved resuscitation and sedation protocol.
Do not delay emergency cardioversion solely to complete routine anticoagulation assessment.
branches.condition: Life-threatening haemodynamic instability attributable to atrial fibrillation

actions: Proceed to symptom, duration, rate/rhythm and thromboembolic-risk assessment.
branches.condition: No life-threatening instability

clinicalManagement.timeframe: Immediately at acute presentation

clinicalManagement.title: Assess stroke and bleeding risks
actions: Use CHA2DS2-VASc for stroke risk and a validated bleeding-risk tool such as ORBIT.
Identify and modify reversible bleeding risks rather than using a bleeding score alone to withhold anticoagulation.
Discuss absolute benefits, bleeding harms and patient preferences using shared decision making.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: At diagnosis and whenever risk factors change

clinicalManagement.title: Prevent thromboembolism
actions: Offer an SFDA-authorised generic direct-acting oral anticoagulant, such as dabigatran etexilate or rivaroxaban, when indicated and suitable; select using renal function, interactions, adherence and the local formulary.
Use warfarin when a direct-acting anticoagulant is contraindicated, unsuitable, or the clinical condition specifically requires a vitamin-K antagonist.
Do not use antiplatelet monotherapy solely for atrial-fibrillation stroke prevention.
Use current SFDA labelling and the local formulary for all dosing; this record is not a prescribing source.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Promptly after risk assessment

clinicalManagement.title: Choose rate or rhythm control
actions: Use rate control first for many stable patients, with a generic beta-blocker or rate-limiting calcium-channel blocker selected for comorbidity and contraindications.
Consider rhythm control for persistent symptoms, a reversible cause, new onset, atrial flutter suitable for ablation or heart failure thought to be driven by the arrhythmia.
Avoid a rate-limiting calcium-channel blocker in acute decompensated heart failure and obtain specialist advice.
Assess anticoagulation requirements around cardioversion according to rhythm duration and the current protocol.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: During initial management and at symptom review

clinicalManagement.title: Escalate persistent or complex disease
actions: Refer for cardiology review when symptoms remain uncontrolled, recurrence follows cardioversion or antiarrhythmic/ablation decisions are needed.
Consider catheter ablation through specialist shared decision making for eligible symptomatic patients.
Reassess stroke prevention after rhythm restoration because apparent sinus rhythm does not automatically remove thromboembolic risk.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Promptly when initial treatment fails or complexity is identified

nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Review symptoms, pulse/rate, blood pressure, anticoagulant adherence, bleeding risk and renal function at a medicine-appropriate interval; reassess stroke risk at least annually and whenever age or comorbidity changes.
mdtReferrals: Cardiology or electrophysiology for rhythm-control and ablation decisions
Anticoagulation or clinical pharmacy service for medicine selection, interactions and adherence
Stroke service for any acute or previous cerebrovascular event
Sleep medicine and weight-management services where relevant
lifestyleAndDiet: Support weight management, regular physical activity and control of blood pressure and diabetes.
Screen for and treat obstructive sleep apnoea when suspected.
Reduce excessive alcohol and stimulant exposure and stop smoking.
For warfarin, advise consistency rather than avoidance of vitamin-K-containing foods and arrange INR education.
patientEducation: Explain the irregular rhythm, symptom-control options and the distinct purpose of anticoagulation.
Teach stroke warning signs and the need for immediate emergency assessment.
Provide medicine-specific bleeding, missed-dose, procedure and interaction advice using approved Saudi information.
dischargeCriteria: Haemodynamics are stable and acute triggers have been addressed.
A rate/rhythm strategy and anticoagulation decision are documented with renal-function-appropriate prescribing.
The patient understands stroke and bleeding precautions and has timely follow-up.

content.title: Breast Cancer Management
content.specialty: Medical Oncology, Breast Surgery and Radiation Oncology

redFlags: Rapidly progressive inflammatory breast change
Spinal pain with weakness, sensory change or bladder/bowel dysfunction
New focal neurological deficit, seizure or raised intracranial-pressure symptoms
Visceral crisis with organ dysfunction requiring rapid oncology assessment
symptoms: New breast or axillary lump
Nipple retraction or bloody discharge
Persistent focal breast change or skin dimpling
Bone pain, breathlessness, neurological symptoms or weight loss in advanced disease
physicalSigns: Discrete breast mass or asymmetric thickening
Peau d'orange, ulceration or inflammatory change
Nipple inversion or eczematous nipple lesion
Palpable axillary or supraclavicular nodes

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Often mobile, well-circumscribed and benign on age-appropriate imaging, but tissue diagnosis is required when assessment is discordant.
Fluid-filled lesion on ultrasound with resolution after aspiration in selected cases.
Pain, erythema, fever and a collection; non-resolution requires investigation for inflammatory malignancy.
History of trauma or surgery with characteristic imaging, although biopsy may be needed if suspicious.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Triple assessment — Breast malignancy
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Concordant suspicious clinical examination, mammography/ultrasound and core-biopsy histology.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Integrates anatomy and tissue diagnosis while minimising false reassurance from any single test.

ruleIn.testName: Histopathology with ER, PR and HER2 testing
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Histopathology with ER, PR and HER2 testing — Invasive breast-cancer subtype
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Malignant morphology with grade and validated receptor status.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Confirms diagnosis and directs endocrine, anti-HER2 and chemotherapy decisions.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Stage-directed imaging — Regional or distant metastatic disease
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Imaging defines tumour, nodal and metastatic burden when stage or symptoms justify it.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Avoids indiscriminate staging in low-risk disease while identifying treatment-changing metastases.

ruleOut.testName: Image-guided core biopsy of a suspicious benign-appearing lesion
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Image-guided core biopsy of a suspicious benign-appearing lesion — Benign breast disease
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Pathology is benign and concordant with clinical and imaging findings.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Benign breast disease
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Discordance requires repeat sampling or excision rather than simple reassurance.

ruleOut.testName: Targeted imaging of new symptoms
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Targeted imaging of new symptoms — Metastatic complication
ruleOut.expectedFinding: No metastasis explaining the symptom, or a lesion is identified for urgent management.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Metastatic complication
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Routine surveillance imaging in asymptomatic early-stage survivors is not a substitute for symptom-led assessment.

pathophysiology.summary: Breast cancer comprises malignant epithelial tumours with heterogeneous hormone-receptor, HER2 and genomic biology. Disease may remain in situ, invade breast and regional lymphatics, or spread haematogenously to bone, liver, lung and brain; biology and stage jointly determine treatment and prognosis.
keyMechanisms: Accumulated genomic and epigenetic alterations enable uncontrolled proliferation and invasion.
Oestrogen/progesterone-receptor signalling and HER2 amplification define actionable biological subsets.
Lymphatic spread commonly involves axillary and regional nodes.
Tumour heterogeneity and treatment selection pressure can change receptor status in recurrent disease.

clinicalManagement.title: Confirm pathology and stage
actions: Obtain adequate core tissue and report histological type, grade and ER, PR and HER2 status.
Complete stage-appropriate imaging and assess performance status, comorbidities and baseline organ function.
Arrange genetic and fertility counselling when clinical criteria are met.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Before definitive treatment

clinicalManagement.title: Agree a multidisciplinary plan
actions: Discuss every new case in a breast multidisciplinary conference.
Integrate stage, biology, patient goals, surgical feasibility and treatment toxicities.
Record sequence of surgery, systemic therapy and radiotherapy with responsible teams.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: After diagnostic work-up

clinicalManagement.title: Deliver local-regional therapy
actions: Offer breast-conserving surgery or mastectomy according to disease extent, contraindications and informed preference.
Stage the axilla using the appropriate sentinel-node or nodal procedure.
Plan radiotherapy according to surgical approach, margins, nodal involvement and recurrence risk.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: According to stage and treatment sequence

clinicalManagement.title: Select biology-directed systemic therapy
actions: Use endocrine therapy for hormone-receptor-positive disease when indicated.
Use generic anti-HER2 therapy for eligible HER2-positive disease with cardiac monitoring.
Select chemotherapy and any contemporary targeted or immunotherapy only through the current approved oncology protocol.
Prioritise neoadjuvant systemic therapy and serial response assessment.
Proceed to local therapy if disease becomes operable and the MDT confirms benefit.
branches.condition: Locally advanced or inflammatory disease

clinicalManagement.timeframe: Neoadjuvant or adjuvant as agreed by MDT

clinicalManagement.title: Survivorship or advanced-disease review
actions: Use interval history, examination and mammography of retained breast tissue according to policy.
Manage endocrine, bone, cardiac, menopausal and lymphoedema effects.
For metastatic disease, prioritise symptom control, quality of life and biology-directed therapy with early supportive care.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: After initial treatment and throughout follow-up

nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Follow the current Saudi oncology surveillance schedule, including clinical review and mammography where breast tissue remains; monitor therapy-specific cardiac, bone, gynaecological and lymphoedema risks and investigate new symptoms promptly.
mdtReferrals: Breast surgeon, medical oncologist, radiation oncologist and breast-care nurse
Genetics for hereditary-risk criteria
Fertility service before gonadotoxic treatment when relevant
Physiotherapy/lymphoedema, psycho-oncology and palliative care according to need
lifestyleAndDiet: Support regular physical activity and maintenance of a healthy body composition during and after treatment.
Provide dietetic advice for treatment-related weight change, nausea or malnutrition.
Offer smoking-cessation support and advise avoidance of unreviewed supplements that may interact with therapy.
patientEducation: Explain stage, receptor status, treatment intent and the role of each modality in plain language.
Discuss expected adverse effects, fertility, sexual health, pregnancy considerations and when to seek urgent care.
Provide individualised information on recurrence symptoms without encouraging harmful routine self-testing.
dischargeCriteria: The diagnosis, stage, receptor profile and MDT plan are documented.
Acute treatment complications are controlled and the patient has clear contacts.
Surveillance ownership, medicine monitoring and urgent symptom pathways are explicit.

title: Breast Cancer Screening Discussion
source_title: Maxcy-Rosenau-Last Public Health and Preventive Medicine, 16th edition

redFlags: New lump, nipple retraction/discharge or skin change is diagnostic assessment, not screening
Strong hereditary pattern or young affected relative
Prior chest irradiation or high-risk lesion
Pregnancy/lactation with new symptom
symptoms: Evaluate the characteristic symptom pattern of Breast Cancer Screening Discussion, including onset, evolution, severity, associated symptoms, precipitating factors, complications, and relevant negative findings.
Clarify onset, progression, associated symptoms, baseline function, medicines and the patient’s own priorities.
Ask about relevant risk factors and context described in the case; document important negative findings rather than assuming their absence.
physicalSigns: Record observations and a focused examination directed to the organ system and competing diagnoses in this topic.
Assess functional change, comorbidity, hydration/perfusion where relevant, and baseline status.
Use serial reassessment when the condition or treatment can change over hours or days.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Needs diagnostic examination/imaging rather than routine screening.
May need genetics and a different imaging pathway.
Still requires assessment based on age and finding.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Screening mammography when eligible — Suspicious breast lesions before symptoms develop
ruleIn.expectedFinding: A recall or abnormal imaging category requires further assessment; a negative screen does not explain a new symptom.
ruleIn.targetCondition: Suspicious breast lesions before symptoms develop
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Detects possible early disease in eligible asymptomatic patients after discussion of benefits and harms.

ruleOut.testName: Structured breast-cancer risk and symptom assessment
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Structured breast-cancer risk and symptom assessment — High-risk family history or a symptom requiring diagnostic assessment
ruleOut.expectedFinding: A lump, skin/nipple change or important hereditary pattern changes the pathway.
ruleOut.targetCondition: High-risk family history or a symptom requiring diagnostic assessment
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Separates asymptomatic screening from symptomatic diagnosis and selects the appropriate Saudi programme or specialist referral.

pathophysiology.summary: Screening aims to detect clinically important cancer earlier in asymptomatic populations but can cause false positives, overdiagnosis, anxiety, and unnecessary procedures. Absolute benefit varies with baseline risk and age. This topic is educational and should be interpreted alongside current local pathways and patient-specific assessment.
keyMechanisms: Screening aims to detect clinically important cancer earlier in asymptomatic populations but can cause false positives, overdiagnosis, anxiety, and unnecessary procedures. Absolute benefit varies with baseline risk and age.
Clinical expression and progression vary with baseline risk, comorbidity, treatment exposure, and access to timely care.

clinicalManagement.title: Assess urgency, stability, and the person’s priorities
actions: Confirm the presenting concern, relevant timeline, baseline function, medicines, allergies, comorbidities, and the patient’s immediate priorities.
Assess the red flags above and use the current local escalation pathway if instability or rapid deterioration is present.
Explain uncertainty and involve the patient or appropriate decision-maker in a way suited to the setting.
Escalate immediately to the responsible senior or emergency team using the local pathway.
Stabilise and investigate in parallel; do not delay time-critical action for routine testing.
branches.condition: A red flag, instability, or rapid deterioration is present

actions: Proceed with focused assessment and shared planning.
Document the threshold for urgent reassessment.
branches.condition: The person is stable for a planned or longitudinal pathway

clinicalManagement.timeframe: At first contact and whenever the situation changes

clinicalManagement.title: Confirm the working diagnosis and stratify risk
actions: Use the history, examination, and investigations listed above to confirm the likely process and assess important alternatives.
Interpret results using current national/local diagnostic criteria, age, pregnancy status, comorbidity, and prior results.
Record severity, uncertainty, and which findings would change the plan.
Reassess the history and examination and seek senior or specialty advice.
Use targeted additional testing only when its result can change management.
branches.condition: The diagnosis remains uncertain or tests conflict with the clinical picture

actions: Switch to the relevant urgent or specialty pathway.
Communicate the finding and handover responsibility clearly.
branches.condition: A high-risk complication or an alternative diagnosis is identified

clinicalManagement.timeframe: Promptly; adapt timing to acuity

clinicalManagement.title: Agree evidence-informed care and address the cause
actions: Use the topic-specific focus in this record to agree immediate and longer-term priorities with the patient.
Select treatment only after checking current local guidance, formulary, contraindications, interactions, organ function, pregnancy considerations, and patient preference.
Treat reversible contributors and address access, communication, cultural, and functional barriers.
Reassess diagnosis, treatment burden, adherence barriers, and alternatives with the responsible specialist.
Document the shared decision and safety-net plan.
branches.condition: Treatment is ineffective, poorly tolerated, or inconsistent with the patient’s goals

actions: Continue the plan with monitoring proportional to risk.
Provide clear instructions for expected course and warning symptoms.
branches.condition: The patient improves on the agreed plan

clinicalManagement.timeframe: According to acuity and current local protocol

clinicalManagement.title: Coordinate handover, education, and follow-up
actions: Provide a written plan stating the working diagnosis, key findings, medicines or interventions, monitoring, and who owns each next step.
Use teach-back to check that the patient or caregiver understands warning symptoms, follow-up, and how to obtain help.
Close the loop on pending results, referrals, and screening or prevention actions.
Arrange a higher level of care or supported transfer and send a structured clinical handover.
Confirm transport, caregiver, and communication needs where relevant.
branches.condition: Safe care cannot be delivered in the current setting

actions: Confirm a feasible follow-up date and contact route.
Document when and how the plan should be reviewed or escalated.
branches.condition: The patient is ready for outpatient or continuing care

clinicalManagement.timeframe: Before transition and at the agreed review interval

nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Review the topic-specific focus, patient goals, symptoms and function at an interval matched to risk. Reconcile new results and treatment effects, close referrals, and revisit the plan if the condition, circumstances, or preferences change.
mdtReferrals: Primary Care / Public Health
Primary care or the responsible continuity team
Pharmacist, nurse educator, dietitian, rehabilitation, mental-health, or social support when relevant to the case.
lifestyleAndDiet: Offer topic-relevant prevention or self-management support that is safe, feasible, culturally appropriate, and consistent with the person’s goals.
Avoid one-size-fits-all restrictions; individualise advice for pregnancy, frailty, kidney/heart disease, disability, and treatment burden.
patientEducation: Explain breast cancer screening discussion in plain language, including what is known, what remains uncertain, and how the plan will be reviewed.
Use teach-back for warning signs, medicines or monitoring, and the route to urgent help.
Invite questions and adapt written or interpreted information to the patient’s language, health literacy, and communication needs.
dischargeCriteria: Clinical status is appropriate for the next setting, and urgent complications have been excluded or addressed.
The patient or caregiver has an understandable plan, access to needed treatment/support, and a clear escalation route.
Pending investigations and referrals have a named owner and follow-up timeframe.

title: Cancer Pain Assessment and Support
source_title: Oxford Textbook of Palliative Medicine, 6th edition

redFlags: New weakness, sensory loss, or bladder/bowel dysfunction
Sudden severe pain suggesting fracture or cord compression
Uncontrolled pain or medication toxicity
New delirium, respiratory suppression, or falls
symptoms: Evaluate the characteristic symptom pattern of Cancer Pain Assessment and Support, including onset, evolution, severity, associated symptoms, precipitating factors, complications, and relevant negative findings.
Clarify onset, progression, associated symptoms, baseline function, medicines and the patient’s own priorities.
Ask about relevant risk factors and context described in the case; document important negative findings rather than assuming their absence.
physicalSigns: Record observations and a focused examination directed to the organ system and competing diagnoses in this topic.
Assess functional change, comorbidity, hydration/perfusion where relevant, and baseline status.
Use serial reassessment when the condition or treatment can change over hours or days.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Burning, shooting, allodynia, or sensory change may indicate nerve involvement.
Movement-related focal pain suggests structural complication.
Temporal relation to therapy or procedure informs cause.

ruleIn.testName: Pain score, pain-character and neurological assessment
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Pain score, pain-character and neurological assessment — Pain severity, neuropathic features and neurological compromise
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Document intensity, interference, neuropathic descriptors and any motor/sensory deficit.
ruleIn.targetCondition: Pain severity, neuropathic features and neurological compromise
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Defines the likely pain mechanism and identifies emergencies such as possible cord compression.

ruleIn.testName: Creatinine and liver tests when prescribing decisions require them
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Creatinine and liver tests when prescribing decisions require them — Impaired drug clearance
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Renal or hepatic dysfunction may increase medicine accumulation and toxicity.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Informs analgesic selection and monitoring under the palliative formulary.

ruleOut.testName: Targeted imaging for suspected structural complication
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Targeted imaging for suspected structural complication — Pathological fracture, spinal cord compression or obstructive disease
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Imaging may show the lesion responsible for focal pain or new neurological signs.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Pathological fracture, spinal cord compression or obstructive disease
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Identifies a treatable complication; choose the modality and urgency for the specific clinical question.

pathophysiology.summary: Cancer pain may arise from tissue injury, inflammation, bone destruction, nerve infiltration, treatment, or interacting mechanisms. Relief requires repeated assessment of both pain and function while minimising adverse effects. This topic is educational and should be interpreted alongside current local pathways and patient-specific assessment.
keyMechanisms: Cancer pain may arise from tissue injury, inflammation, bone destruction, nerve infiltration, treatment, or interacting mechanisms. Relief requires repeated assessment of both pain and function while minimising adverse effects.
Clinical expression and progression vary with baseline risk, comorbidity, treatment exposure, and access to timely care.

title: Cardiovascular Risk Assessment
source_title: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd edition

redFlags: Chest pain, focal neurological symptoms or exertional syncope require diagnostic assessment
Severe hypertension with acute organ symptoms
Known vascular disease shifts to secondary prevention
Very high inherited lipid risk
symptoms: Evaluate the characteristic symptom pattern of Cardiovascular Risk Assessment, including onset, evolution, severity, associated symptoms, precipitating factors, complications, and relevant negative findings.
Clarify onset, progression, associated symptoms, baseline function, medicines and the patient’s own priorities.
Ask about relevant risk factors and context described in the case; document important negative findings rather than assuming their absence.
physicalSigns: Record observations and a focused examination directed to the organ system and competing diagnoses in this topic.
Assess functional change, comorbidity, hydration/perfusion where relevant, and baseline status.
Use serial reassessment when the condition or treatment can change over hours or days.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Prior cardiovascular event has a different risk and treatment framework.
Marked LDL and family pattern warrant evaluation.
Confirm with appropriate repeat or out-of-office measures.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Standardised blood-pressure measurement — Sustained elevated blood pressure
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Repeated readings and out-of-office confirmation distinguish persistent elevation from measurement effects.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Provides an accurate modifiable-risk measure for the overall cardiovascular assessment.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Lipid profile — Atherogenic lipid burden
ruleIn.expectedFinding: LDL and other lipid fractions inform risk estimation and possible inherited dyslipidaemia.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Supports prevention decisions alongside age, smoking, diabetes and established vascular disease.

ruleOut.testName: HbA1c or fasting glucose and kidney assessment when indicated
ruleOut.modalityTarget: HbA1c or fasting glucose and kidney assessment when indicated — Diabetes or chronic kidney disease modifying cardiovascular risk
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Abnormal glycaemia, reduced filtration or albuminuria changes risk categorisation.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Diabetes or chronic kidney disease modifying cardiovascular risk
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Identifies important comorbidity; use a locally accepted risk method and confirm abnormalities appropriately.

pathophysiology.summary: Atherosclerotic events arise from cumulative vascular exposure and thrombosis; risk-factor combinations alter absolute event probability. Preventive benefit should be judged against baseline risk, treatment burden, and patient preferences. This topic is educational and should be interpreted alongside current local pathways and patient-specific assessment.
keyMechanisms: Atherosclerotic events arise from cumulative vascular exposure and thrombosis
risk-factor combinations alter absolute event probability. Preventive benefit should be judged against baseline risk, treatment burden, and patient preferences.

title: Cataract Surgery Assessment and Preparation
source_title: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd edition

redFlags: Sudden visual loss or painful red eye is not routine cataract
Retinal disease or optic neuropathy may limit visual gain
Active ocular infection
Unclear capacity or unrealistic expectations requiring discussion
symptoms: Evaluate the characteristic symptom pattern of Cataract Surgery Assessment and Preparation, including onset, evolution, severity, associated symptoms, precipitating factors, complications, and relevant negative findings.
Clarify onset, progression, associated symptoms, baseline function, medicines and the patient’s own priorities.
Ask about relevant risk factors and context described in the case; document important negative findings rather than assuming their absence.
physicalSigns: Record observations and a focused examination directed to the organ system and competing diagnoses in this topic.
Assess functional change, comorbidity, hydration/perfusion where relevant, and baseline status.
Use serial reassessment when the condition or treatment can change over hours or days.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Refraction may improve symptoms without surgery.
May be the limiting cause of visual impairment.
May require separate or combined planning.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Visual acuity and slit-lamp examination — Lens opacity and its effect on vision
ruleIn.expectedFinding: A cataract consistent with symptoms supports the diagnosis; acuity alone does not establish the cause.
ruleIn.targetCondition: Lens opacity and its effect on vision
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Determines whether cataract is the main source of visual disability and whether surgery is likely to help.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Ocular biometry — Measurements needed for intraocular-lens selection
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Axial length and corneal measurements guide lens-power calculation.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Supports surgical planning and reduces avoidable refractive error.

ruleOut.testName: Retinal and optic-nerve assessment
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Retinal and optic-nerve assessment — Other ocular disease limiting postoperative vision
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Macular, retinal or optic-nerve abnormalities may reduce the expected benefit.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Other ocular disease limiting postoperative vision
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Identifies competing causes of poor vision and informs consent and referral.

pathophysiology.summary: Lens opacity scatters light and reduces visual function; surgery replaces the opaque lens with an intraocular implant. Benefit depends on cataract contribution, ocular comorbidity, refractive goals, and safe perioperative care. This topic is educational and should be interpreted alongside current local pathways and patient-specific assessment.
keyMechanisms: Lens opacity scatters light and reduces visual function
surgery replaces the opaque lens with an intraocular implant. Benefit depends on cataract contribution, ocular comorbidity, refractive goals, and safe perioperative care.

Severe hyperkalaemia or acidosis
Pulmonary oedema or uraemic symptoms

ruleOut.targetCondition: Intrinsic kidney disease or obstruction
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Identifies a potentially treatable cause and helps distinguish chronic disease from a new reversible process.

title: Community-Acquired Pneumonia
source_title: Lower Respiratory Tract Infections Management Protocol

content.title: Community-Acquired Pneumonia
content.specialty: Internal Medicine, Respiratory Medicine and Infectious Diseases

redFlags: Respiratory failure, exhaustion or rapidly increasing oxygen need
Shock, altered mental status, oliguria or other sepsis-associated organ dysfunction
Multilobar disease, cavitation or a large pleural effusion
Immunocompromise, aspiration risk or failure to improve on appropriate initial therapy
symptoms: Acute cough with or without sputum
Fever, rigors or malaise
Dyspnoea or pleuritic chest pain
Confusion or functional decline, especially in older adults
physicalSigns: Tachypnoea, hypoxaemia or increased work of breathing
Focal crackles, bronchial breathing or dullness to percussion
Fever or hypothermia with tachycardia
Confusion, hypotension or poor perfusion in severe disease

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Abrupt pleuritic pain or dyspnoea, thrombosis risk and limited infective prodrome; imaging shows vascular rather than air-space disease.
Orthopnoea, bilateral congestion, raised jugular venous pressure and cardiac dysfunction.
Diffuse upper-respiratory features without focal consolidation or compatible chest imaging.
Subacute constitutional symptoms, epidemiologic risk, upper-lobe or cavitary change and specific microbiology.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Chest radiograph — Pulmonary air-space infection
ruleIn.expectedFinding: New focal or multifocal infiltrate compatible with pneumonia.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Supports diagnosis, extent assessment and detection of effusion or another thoracic process in hospital-managed disease.

ruleIn.testName: Pulse oximetry and blood gas when severe
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Pulse oximetry and blood gas when severe — Gas-exchange impairment
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Hypoxaemia, with acidaemia or ventilatory failure in advanced disease.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Determines oxygen and ventilatory support needs.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Microbiology selected by severity — Causative pathogen
ruleIn.expectedFinding: A plausible bacterial or viral pathogen in good-quality respiratory, blood or molecular samples.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Severe or epidemiologically important disease benefits most from organism identification and antimicrobial narrowing.

ruleOut.testName: Electrocardiogram and cardiac assessment
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Electrocardiogram and cardiac assessment — Heart failure or acute coronary syndrome
ruleOut.expectedFinding: No primary cardiac process sufficient to explain the presentation.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Heart failure or acute coronary syndrome
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Cardiac disease commonly mimics or coexists with pneumonia.

ruleOut.testName: CT chest or pleural ultrasound when indicated
ruleOut.modalityTarget: CT chest or pleural ultrasound when indicated — Pulmonary embolism, malignancy, abscess or complicated effusion
ruleOut.expectedFinding: No alternative lesion, or a complication is identified for targeted management.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Pulmonary embolism, malignancy, abscess or complicated effusion
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Reserved for diagnostic uncertainty, complication assessment or treatment failure.

pathophysiology.summary: Community-acquired pneumonia is infection of the distal airways and alveoli acquired outside hospital or early after admission. Alveolar inflammation and exudate impair ventilation and gas exchange; systemic inflammatory effects may cause sepsis and organ dysfunction.
keyMechanisms: Pathogen aspiration or inhalation overcomes airway and innate immune defences.
Alveolar neutrophilic inflammation and fluid cause consolidation and ventilation-perfusion mismatch.
Host response varies with age, comorbidity, immune status and pathogen virulence.
Complications include parapneumonic effusion, empyema, lung abscess, respiratory failure and sepsis.

clinicalManagement.title: Confirm diagnosis and assess severity
actions: Assess oxygenation, sepsis features, comorbidity and ability to take oral treatment.
Use a validated severity tool as an adjunct, not a replacement for clinical judgement.
Identify aspiration, resistant-organism, travel and immunocompromise risks.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: At presentation

clinicalManagement.title: Start empiric antimicrobial therapy
actions: Select generic therapy from the current MOH/local formulary according to severity, allergy, recent exposure and the local antibiogram.
Obtain indicated cultures first only when this will not delay urgent therapy.
Document indication, route, review date and planned duration.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Promptly after diagnosis; immediately when sepsis or shock is present

clinicalManagement.title: Provide supportive care
actions: Titrate oxygen to the appropriate clinical target.
Treat sepsis, fluid deficit, pain and fever while accounting for cardiac and renal status.
Provide thrombosis prevention and early mobilisation for admitted patients when appropriate.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Concurrent with antimicrobial treatment

clinicalManagement.title: Review response and complications
actions: Reassess observations, oxygen need, mental status, oral intake and inflammatory/organ-function trends.
Narrow or change antimicrobials using microbiology and clinical response.
Investigate empyema, abscess, resistant pathogen, obstruction or an alternative diagnosis when improvement is absent.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Formal review within 24 to 48 hours or sooner if deteriorating

clinicalManagement.title: Switch route and plan discharge
actions: Switch from intravenous to oral treatment when stability and gastrointestinal absorption permit.
Use the shortest effective guideline-concordant course and document the stop date.
Arrange follow-up imaging only for persistent symptoms or guideline-defined risk, not automatically for every patient.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: When clinically stable

nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Arrange clinical review based on severity and comorbidity; follow pending cultures, reassess non-resolution, and consider interval chest imaging for persistent symptoms or higher malignancy risk according to local policy.
mdtReferrals: Critical care for respiratory failure or shock
Respiratory medicine for complications, recurrent pneumonia or diagnostic uncertainty
Microbiology or infectious diseases for resistant organisms, severe immunocompromise or treatment failure
Speech and language therapy for suspected aspiration
lifestyleAndDiet: Encourage hydration and nutrition as tolerated.
Offer smoking-cessation support.
Review influenza, pneumococcal and other indicated vaccination after recovery.
patientEducation: Explain the expected recovery trajectory and that cough and fatigue may outlast fever.
Give return precautions for worsening breathlessness, confusion, cyanosis, chest pain or inability to maintain intake.
Explain antimicrobial adherence and why unused antibiotics should not be saved or shared.
dischargeCriteria: Vital signs and oxygen requirement are stable at an appropriate baseline.
The patient can take oral medicine and maintain hydration and nutrition.
A safe antimicrobial plan, follow-up ownership and return precautions are documented.

title: Conservative Kidney Care Planning
source_title: Oxford Textbook of Palliative Medicine, 6th edition

redFlags: Refractory fluid overload, hyperkalaemia, acidosis, or uraemic symptoms needing urgent review
Conflict or uncertainty about capacity and preferences
Uncontrolled pain, pruritus, nausea, or breathlessness
Caregiver inability to sustain home plan
symptoms: Evaluate the characteristic symptom pattern of Conservative Kidney Care Planning, including onset, evolution, severity, associated symptoms, precipitating factors, complications, and relevant negative findings.
Clarify onset, progression, associated symptoms, baseline function, medicines and the patient’s own priorities.
Ask about relevant risk factors and context described in the case; document important negative findings rather than assuming their absence.
physicalSigns: Record observations and a focused examination directed to the organ system and competing diagnoses in this topic.
Assess functional change, comorbidity, hydration/perfusion where relevant, and baseline status.
Use serial reassessment when the condition or treatment can change over hours or days.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Assess and treat when consistent with goals.
Offer support before interpreting preference.
Present options without coercion.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Symptom, function and goals-of-care assessment — Uraemic symptom burden and priorities
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Document pruritus, nausea, breathlessness, function and the person's preferred care limits.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Aligns monitoring and interventions with comfort and shared decisions.

ruleIn.testName: Potassium, bicarbonate and creatinine when results will change care
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Potassium, bicarbonate and creatinine when results will change care — Electrolyte/acidosis complications and kidney trajectory
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Abnormal potassium/bicarbonate or a changing filtration trend may explain symptoms and identify treatment options.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Uses proportionate testing for manageable complications rather than routine burdensome testing without a decision.

ruleOut.testName: Focused examination and medication review after new deterioration
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Focused examination and medication review after new deterioration — Fluid overload, infection or drug-related harm
ruleOut.expectedFinding: A new focal finding or exposure directs additional investigation.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Fluid overload, infection or drug-related harm
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Identifies reversible problems within the agreed conservative-care plan.

pathophysiology.summary: Advanced kidney disease causes fluid, electrolyte, metabolic, and uraemic symptoms. Conservative kidney management is active care focused on symptoms, function, and quality of life when dialysis is not chosen or is unlikely to meet patient goals. This topic is educational and should be interpreted alongside current local pathways and patient-specific assessment.
keyMechanisms: Advanced kidney disease causes fluid, electrolyte, metabolic, and uraemic symptoms. Conservative kidney management is active care focused on symptoms, function, and quality of life when dialysis is not chosen or is unlikely to meet patient goals.
Clinical expression and progression vary with baseline risk, comorbidity, treatment exposure, and access to timely care.

title: Deep-Vein Thrombosis and Pulmonary Embolism
source_title: MOH DVT and Pulmonary Embolism Treatment Protocols

content.title: Deep-Vein Thrombosis and Pulmonary Embolism
content.specialty: Emergency Medicine, Internal Medicine and Haematology

redFlags: Haemodynamic instability, syncope with persistent hypotension or obstructive-shock features
Severe hypoxaemia, rapidly escalating oxygen requirement or cardiac arrest
Threatened limb with massive swelling, cyanosis or severe pain
Active major bleeding or another absolute barrier to anticoagulation in a patient with confirmed or highly suspected VTE
symptoms: Unilateral leg pain or swelling
Sudden unexplained dyspnoea
Pleuritic chest pain, cough, haemoptysis or syncope
Reduced exercise tolerance with recent immobility, surgery, cancer or prior thrombosis
physicalSigns: Unilateral pitting oedema, calf asymmetry or deep venous tenderness
Tachycardia, tachypnoea or hypoxaemia
Signs of right-heart strain such as raised jugular venous pressure
Hypotension or poor perfusion in high-risk pulmonary embolism

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Superficial erythema, warmth and a possible portal of entry with inflammatory features rather than isolated deep venous tenderness.
Posterior knee pathology with fluid tracking into the calf and diagnostic ultrasound findings.
Pressure-type pain, ischaemic electrocardiographic change or a coronary biomarker pattern rather than pleuritic pain and right-heart strain.
Focal infective symptoms or unilateral absent breath sounds with confirmatory chest imaging.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Compression ultrasonography — Proximal lower-limb DVT
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Non-compressible venous segment or directly visualised thrombus.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: First-line anatomical confirmation for suspected proximal DVT.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: CT pulmonary angiography — Pulmonary embolism
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Intraluminal filling defect in a pulmonary artery.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Confirms pulmonary embolism and describes clot burden while also identifying some alternative thoracic diagnoses.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Echocardiography in unstable PE — Right-ventricular pressure overload
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Right-ventricular dilatation or dysfunction compatible with acute pressure overload.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Supports urgent risk stratification when instability makes definitive imaging unsafe or delayed.

ruleOut.testName: High-sensitivity D-dimer in an appropriate low-probability pathway
ruleOut.modalityTarget: High-sensitivity D-dimer in an appropriate low-probability pathway — Acute VTE
ruleOut.expectedFinding: A negative result below the assay's validated threshold makes acute VTE unlikely in the selected population.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Acute VTE
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Avoids unnecessary imaging only after structured clinical-probability assessment.

ruleOut.testName: Ventilation-perfusion imaging
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Ventilation-perfusion imaging — Pulmonary embolism when CTPA is unsuitable
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Normal perfusion argues strongly against PE; a mismatched perfusion defect supports it.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Pulmonary embolism when CTPA is unsuitable
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Provides an alternative when contrast, radiation distribution or renal considerations make CTPA unsuitable.

pathophysiology.summary: Venous thromboembolism results from venous stasis, endothelial injury and hypercoagulability. A deep-vein thrombus may obstruct limb venous return or embolise to pulmonary arteries, increasing dead space and pulmonary vascular resistance and, in severe cases, causing right-ventricular failure and shock.
keyMechanisms: Thrombus formation is promoted by immobility, surgery, cancer, oestrogen exposure, pregnancy and inherited or acquired thrombophilia.
Pulmonary arterial obstruction produces ventilation-perfusion mismatch and hypoxaemia.
Acute right-ventricular pressure overload can reduce left-ventricular filling and systemic cardiac output.
Residual venous obstruction and valve damage contribute to post-thrombotic syndrome; persistent vascular obstruction may cause chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension.

clinicalManagement.title: Estimate clinical probability
actions: Use a validated DVT or PE clinical-probability tool within its intended population.
Check haemodynamic stability and bleeding risk before selecting the diagnostic pathway.
Do not use a D-dimer to rule out VTE when clinical probability is high.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: At first assessment

clinicalManagement.title: Obtain definitive imaging
actions: Arrange compression ultrasonography for suspected DVT and CTPA or appropriate ventilation-perfusion imaging for suspected PE.
Give interim therapeutic anticoagulation when indicated by the approved pathway and imaging is delayed, after checking contraindications.
Obtain baseline blood count, renal and liver function, coagulation studies and pregnancy testing when relevant without delaying urgent treatment.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Urgently according to probability and stability

clinicalManagement.title: Start anticoagulation
actions: Select a locally formulary-approved anticoagulant based on renal and hepatic function, cancer, pregnancy potential, interactions, bleeding risk and patient preference.
Use generic agents and approved dosing references; do not derive dosing from this data record.
Document intended duration and the review point for extension or cessation.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Once VTE is confirmed or interim treatment is indicated

clinicalManagement.title: Manage high-risk pulmonary embolism
actions: Activate critical-care and senior specialist support for haemodynamic instability.
Consider systemic thrombolysis or another reperfusion strategy only after rapid assessment of contraindications and local capability.
Provide respiratory and circulatory support while definitive therapy is organised.
Seek urgent haematology or vascular advice.
Consider a temporary mechanical strategy only when guideline criteria are met, with an explicit retrieval plan.
branches.condition: Anticoagulation is contraindicated

clinicalManagement.timeframe: Immediately

clinicalManagement.title: Plan secondary prevention
actions: Classify the event as provoked, unprovoked or cancer-associated and document persistent risk factors.
Review adherence, interactions and bleeding precautions.
Avoid routine thrombophilia testing when it will not change management; seek specialist advice for selected cases.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Before discharge

nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Review early after discharge for symptoms, bleeding, adherence and renal function where relevant; reassess treatment duration at the guideline-defined milestone and investigate persistent dyspnoea for post-PE complications.
mdtReferrals: Haematology for recurrent, unusual-site or selected unprovoked VTE
Oncology for suspected or active cancer-associated thrombosis
Vascular or interventional service for threatened limb or selected reperfusion decisions
Obstetric medicine for pregnancy or postpartum VTE
lifestyleAndDiet: Encourage mobilisation as tolerated once anticoagulation and clinical stability permit.
Reduce prolonged immobility during travel and recovery and maintain hydration when appropriate.
Address smoking, obesity and other modifiable vascular risks without implying that lifestyle replaces anticoagulation.

title: Delirium and Agitation Near End of Life
source_title: Oxford Textbook of Palliative Medicine, 6th edition

content.title: Delirium and Agitation Near End of Life

redFlags: Seizure, focal deficit, or sudden severe headache
Respiratory compromise or suspected toxicity
Unsafe agitation or risk of injury
Family distress with unresolved goals or uncertainty
symptoms: Evaluate the characteristic symptom pattern of Delirium and Agitation Near End of Life, including onset, evolution, severity, associated symptoms, precipitating factors, complications, and relevant negative findings.
Clarify onset, progression, associated symptoms, baseline function, medicines and the patient’s own priorities.
Ask about relevant risk factors and context described in the case; document important negative findings rather than assuming their absence.
physicalSigns: Record observations and a focused examination directed to the organ system and competing diagnoses in this topic.
Assess functional change, comorbidity, hydration/perfusion where relevant, and baseline status.
Use serial reassessment when the condition or treatment can change over hours or days.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Acute fluctuation and inattention suggest delirium over baseline decline.
May coexist but does not explain acute altered attention alone.

differentials.condition: Medication toxicity, infection, retention, constipation, dehydration
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Common reversible contributors to assess.

ruleIn.testName: Collateral history and validated delirium assessment
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Collateral history and validated delirium assessment — Acute fluctuating inattention or cognitive change
ruleIn.expectedFinding: A change from baseline with fluctuation and impaired attention supports delirium.
ruleIn.targetCondition: Acute fluctuating inattention or cognitive change
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Distinguishes delirium from chronic cognitive impairment and establishes the time course.

ruleOut.testName: Pain, bladder, bowel and medication assessment
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Pain, bladder, bowel and medication assessment — Reversible causes of distress
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Pain, retention, constipation or a recent deliriogenic medicine may explain agitation.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Reversible causes of distress
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Detects treatable contributors without automatically adding invasive investigations.

ruleOut.testName: Targeted glucose, electrolytes or infection tests when goal-concordant
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Targeted glucose, electrolytes or infection tests when goal-concordant — A suspected metabolic or infectious precipitant
ruleOut.expectedFinding: An abnormal result is interpreted against the suspected cause and goals of care.
ruleOut.targetCondition: A suspected metabolic or infectious precipitant
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Order only the named tests likely to change symptom-focused treatment.

pathophysiology.summary: Delirium is an acute disturbance of attention and awareness caused by interacting vulnerability and precipitating factors. Near end of life, illness, medicines, dehydration, pain, retention, and environment may contribute. This topic is educational and should be interpreted alongside current local pathways and patient-specific assessment.
keyMechanisms: Delirium is an acute disturbance of attention and awareness caused by interacting vulnerability and precipitating factors. Near end of life, illness, medicines, dehydration, pain, retention, and environment may contribute.
Clinical expression and progression vary with baseline risk, comorbidity, treatment exposure, and access to timely care.
