title: Diabetes Screening in At-Risk Adults
source_title: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd edition

redFlags: Classic symptoms with marked glucose elevation require prompt diagnostic assessment
Pregnancy or recent gestational diabetes has separate follow-up needs
Rapid weight loss or ketosis needs urgent evaluation
Discordant tests require clinical interpretation
symptoms: Evaluate the characteristic symptom pattern of Diabetes Screening in At-Risk Adults, including onset, evolution, severity, associated symptoms, precipitating factors, complications, and relevant negative findings.
Clarify onset, progression, associated symptoms, baseline function, medicines and the patient’s own priorities.
Ask about relevant risk factors and context described in the case; document important negative findings rather than assuming their absence.
physicalSigns: Record observations and a focused examination directed to the organ system and competing diagnoses in this topic.
Assess functional change, comorbidity, hydration/perfusion where relevant, and baseline status.
Use serial reassessment when the condition or treatment can change over hours or days.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Repeat testing after acute illness if appropriate.
Review glucocorticoids and other risks.
Symptoms, ketosis, or rapid progression changes urgency.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Laboratory HbA1c when appropriate — Chronic hyperglycaemia
ruleIn.expectedFinding: An elevated result requires interpretation using the adopted diagnostic pathway; altered red-cell turnover can make it unreliable.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Assesses longer-term glycaemia without fasting when the assay is suitable for the patient.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Fasting plasma glucose — Fasting hyperglycaemia
ruleIn.expectedFinding: An abnormal fasting value supports dysglycaemia and may require confirmation if the patient is asymptomatic.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Provides a glucose-based assessment when HbA1c is unsuitable or as an alternative screening method.

ruleOut.testName: Repeat diagnostic testing when required
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Repeat diagnostic testing when required — Persistent rather than isolated hyperglycaemia
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Concordant abnormal laboratory results confirm persistence according to the adopted criteria.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Persistent rather than isolated hyperglycaemia
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Reduces misclassification from biological variation, acute illness or testing error.

pathophysiology.summary: Type 2 diabetes often develops gradually through insulin resistance and beta-cell dysfunction, allowing a period of asymptomatic dysglycaemia. Screening aims to identify people likely to benefit from preventive support and earlier care. This topic is educational and should be interpreted alongside current local pathways and patient-specific assessment.
keyMechanisms: Type 2 diabetes often develops gradually through insulin resistance and beta-cell dysfunction, allowing a period of asymptomatic dysglycaemia. Screening aims to identify people likely to benefit from preventive support and earlier care.
Clinical expression and progression vary with baseline risk, comorbidity, treatment exposure, and access to timely care.

title: Diabetic Ketoacidosis
source_title: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd edition

redFlags: Shock or severe dehydration
Reduced consciousness or inability to protect airway
Severe acidosis or dangerous potassium disturbance
Pregnancy or suspected cerebral injury
symptoms: Evaluate the characteristic symptom pattern of Diabetic Ketoacidosis, including onset, evolution, severity, associated symptoms, precipitating factors, complications, and relevant negative findings.
Clarify onset, progression, associated symptoms, baseline function, medicines and the patient’s own priorities.
Ask about relevant risk factors and context described in the case; document important negative findings rather than assuming their absence.
physicalSigns: Record observations and a focused examination directed to the organ system and competing diagnoses in this topic.
Assess functional change, comorbidity, hydration/perfusion where relevant, and baseline status.
Use serial reassessment when the condition or treatment can change over hours or days.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: More profound hyperosmolality and usually less prominent ketosis/acidosis; mixed presentations occur.
Exposure history and biochemical pattern differ.
May precipitate crisis or coexist; do not attribute all pain to DKA.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Blood glucose and blood ketones — Hyperglycaemia and ketonaemia
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Raised ketones with the clinical context support DKA; glucose may be less elevated in euglycaemic DKA.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Detects the metabolic emergency and tracks ketone resolution alongside acid-base results.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Venous blood gas and electrolytes — Metabolic acidosis and potassium disturbance
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Reduced pH/bicarbonate with ketonaemia supports ketoacidosis; measured potassium may mask total-body depletion.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Defines severity and guides safe treatment and monitoring under the current Saudi DKA protocol.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Creatinine and fluid-balance assessment — Dehydration and kidney impairment
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Renal deterioration and fluid-balance changes help define volume loss and treatment tolerance.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Supports individualised fluid management and complication surveillance.

ruleOut.testName: ECG and source-directed infection tests when indicated
ruleOut.modalityTarget: ECG and source-directed infection tests when indicated — A cardiac/infectious precipitant or electrolyte-related arrhythmia
ruleOut.expectedFinding: ECG abnormalities or a positive source investigation directs parallel management; avoid indiscriminate cultures.
ruleOut.targetCondition: A cardiac/infectious precipitant or electrolyte-related arrhythmia
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Identifies and treats the trigger without delaying the metabolic emergency pathway.

pathophysiology.summary: Insulin deficiency and counter-regulatory hormones increase lipolysis and hepatic ketone production; osmotic diuresis produces water and electrolyte loss. Infection, interrupted insulin, new diabetes, medicines, or acute stress may precipitate crisis. This topic is educational and should be interpreted alongside current local pathways and patient-specific assessment.
keyMechanisms: Insulin deficiency and counter-regulatory hormones increase lipolysis and hepatic ketone production
osmotic diuresis produces water and electrolyte loss. Infection, interrupted insulin, new diabetes, medicines, or acute stress may precipitate crisis.

title: Dyslipidaemia and Atherosclerotic Risk
source_title: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd edition

redFlags: Acute chest pain or stroke symptoms
Severe lipid elevation with abdominal pain suggesting pancreatitis
Family history of premature vascular events
Tendon xanthomas or corneal arcus with very high LDL
symptoms: Evaluate the characteristic symptom pattern of Dyslipidaemia and Atherosclerotic Risk, including onset, evolution, severity, associated symptoms, precipitating factors, complications, and relevant negative findings.
Clarify onset, progression, associated symptoms, baseline function, medicines and the patient’s own priorities.

physicalSigns: Record observations and a focused examination directed to the organ system and competing diagnoses in this topic.
Assess functional change, comorbidity, hydration/perfusion where relevant, and baseline status.
Use serial reassessment when the condition or treatment can change over hours or days.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Marked LDL and family history support inherited-risk evaluation.
Diabetes, thyroid, renal/liver disease, alcohol, and medicines can contribute.
Repeat or clarify sampling if result conflicts with clinical context.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Lipid profile — LDL elevation and triglyceride abnormality
ruleIn.expectedFinding: The lipid pattern and degree of elevation inform risk and possible inherited disease.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Provides the baseline for prevention decisions and later response assessment.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Family history and vascular-risk assessment — Premature atherosclerosis or familial dyslipidaemia
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Premature events, markedly elevated historical LDL or affected relatives may warrant specialist evaluation.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Determines prevention intensity and whether family assessment is appropriate.

ruleOut.testName: TSH, glycaemia, renal or liver tests when a secondary cause is suspected
ruleOut.modalityTarget: TSH, glycaemia, renal or liver tests when a secondary cause is suspected — Hypothyroidism, diabetes or organ disease contributing to dyslipidaemia
ruleOut.expectedFinding: A relevant biochemical abnormality redirects assessment to a secondary contributor.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Hypothyroidism, diabetes or organ disease contributing to dyslipidaemia
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Tests the specific suspected cause rather than assuming all abnormal lipids are primary.

Absolute preventive benefit depends on baseline risk, lipid level, treatment intensity, competing risks, and patient preference. This topic is educational and should be interpreted alongside current local pathways and patient-specific assessment.

Clinical expression and progression vary with baseline risk, comorbidity, treatment exposure, and access to timely care.

title: Elective Coronary Revascularisation Review
source_title: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd edition

redFlags: Acute coronary syndrome or rest pain
Decompensated heart failure
Unstable arrhythmia or severe renal injury
Active infection before an elective procedure
symptoms: Evaluate the characteristic symptom pattern of Elective Coronary Revascularisation Review, including onset, evolution, severity, associated symptoms, precipitating factors, complications, and relevant negative findings.
Clarify onset, progression, associated symptoms, baseline function, medicines and the patient’s own priorities.
Ask about relevant risk factors and context described in the case; document important negative findings rather than assuming their absence.
physicalSigns: Record observations and a focused examination directed to the organ system and competing diagnoses in this topic.
Assess functional change, comorbidity, hydration/perfusion where relevant, and baseline status.
Use serial reassessment when the condition or treatment can change over hours or days.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Reassess symptoms and objective evidence.
Epicardial anatomy may not fully explain symptoms.
Pattern and response differ; specialist review may be needed.

ruleIn.testName: Review of coronary angiography and ischaemia evidence
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Review of coronary angiography and ischaemia evidence — Coronary anatomy and clinically important ischaemia
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Anatomical stenoses and functional evidence are assessed together; anatomy alone does not establish benefit from intervention.
ruleIn.targetCondition: Coronary anatomy and clinically important ischaemia
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Supports Heart Team selection of revascularisation strategy and shared consent.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Echocardiography — Ventricular function and associated valve disease
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Systolic dysfunction or important valve pathology influences procedural risk and planning.
ruleIn.targetCondition: Ventricular function and associated valve disease
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Defines cardiac function before the proposed intervention.

ruleOut.testName: Full blood count, creatinine and medication review
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Full blood count, creatinine and medication review — Anaemia, kidney dysfunction and bleeding/antithrombotic risk
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Anaemia or impaired kidney function may require optimisation; document antiplatelet and anticoagulant exposure.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Anaemia, kidney dysfunction and bleeding/antithrombotic risk
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Plans safe contrast/procedural care and avoids preventable bleeding or medicine interruption.

title: Elective Hernia Repair Assessment
source_title: Sabiston Textbook of Surgery: The Biological Basis of Modern Surgical Practice, 22nd edition

redFlags: Irreducible painful bulge with vomiting
Skin change, fever, or bowel obstruction
Acute testicular pain or vascular compromise
Rapid enlargement or unclear diagnosis
symptoms: Evaluate the characteristic symptom pattern of Elective Hernia Repair Assessment, including onset, evolution, severity, associated symptoms, precipitating factors, complications, and relevant negative findings.
Clarify onset, progression, associated symptoms, baseline function, medicines and the patient’s own priorities.
Ask about relevant risk factors and context described in the case; document important negative findings rather than assuming their absence.
physicalSigns: Record observations and a focused examination directed to the organ system and competing diagnoses in this topic.
Assess functional change, comorbidity, hydration/perfusion where relevant, and baseline status.
Use serial reassessment when the condition or treatment can change over hours or days.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Examination and ultrasound may distinguish from hernia.
Pulsatility requires vascular assessment.
Anatomy and imaging clarify diagnosis.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Standing and supine groin/abdominal examination — Hernia location, reducibility and complication signs
ruleIn.expectedFinding: A cough impulse or reducible bulge supports hernia; painful irreducibility requires urgent assessment.
ruleIn.targetCondition: Hernia location, reducibility and complication signs
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Defines the clinical diagnosis and separates an elective case from possible incarceration or strangulation.

ruleOut.testName: Ultrasound when examination is inconclusive
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Ultrasound when examination is inconclusive — An occult hernia or alternative groin mass
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Dynamic imaging may demonstrate a defect or another lesion.
ruleOut.targetCondition: An occult hernia or alternative groin mass
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Clarifies uncertain anatomy rather than routinely imaging every clinically evident hernia.

ruleOut.testName: Targeted anaesthetic and medication assessment
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Targeted anaesthetic and medication assessment — Modifiable perioperative risk
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Cardiopulmonary disease, anticoagulation or impaired functional status directs specific additional testing.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Modifiable perioperative risk
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Selects preoperative tests according to comorbidity and planned anaesthesia.

title: Elective Hip and Knee Arthroplasty Preparation
source_title: Sabiston Textbook of Surgery: The Biological Basis of Modern Surgical Practice, 22nd edition

content.title: Elective Hip and Knee Arthroplasty Preparation

redFlags: Active infection or skin lesion near operative site
Unstable cardiac/pulmonary disease
Uncontrolled glycaemia or severe anaemia needing optimisation
New calf swelling or acute joint change before surgery
symptoms: Evaluate the characteristic symptom pattern of Elective Hip and Knee Arthroplasty Preparation, including onset, evolution, severity, associated symptoms, precipitating factors, complications, and relevant negative findings.
Clarify onset, progression, associated symptoms, baseline function, medicines and the patient’s own priorities.
Ask about relevant risk factors and context described in the case; document important negative findings rather than assuming their absence.
physicalSigns: Record observations and a focused examination directed to the organ system and competing diagnoses in this topic.
Assess functional change, comorbidity, hydration/perfusion where relevant, and baseline status.
Use serial reassessment when the condition or treatment can change over hours or days.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Examination and imaging should confirm symptom source.
May alter procedure and perioperative medicines.
May affect expected benefit and rehabilitation plan.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Joint radiographs and functional assessment — Structural joint disease matching symptoms
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Degenerative change and documented disability are considered together; radiographic severity alone does not determine the need for surgery.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Confirms the indication and supports shared expectations about benefit.

ruleIn.testName: Full blood count and renal/metabolic tests when indicated
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Full blood count and renal/metabolic tests when indicated — Anaemia and organ dysfunction requiring optimisation
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Low haemoglobin or renal/metabolic abnormalities may alter preparation.
ruleIn.targetCondition: Anaemia and organ dysfunction requiring optimisation
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Identifies treatable perioperative risks under the local preoperative pathway.

ruleOut.testName: Infection, skin and medication assessment
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Infection, skin and medication assessment — Active infection or medication-related surgical risk
ruleOut.expectedFinding: An active infection, wound problem or relevant medicine exposure requires review.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Active infection or medication-related surgical risk
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Reduces avoidable postoperative complications and selects further tests only for identified concerns.

pathophysiology.summary: Advanced joint degeneration produces pain, stiffness, and impaired function; arthroplasty may improve pain and mobility in selected patients. Outcomes depend on comorbidity optimisation, infection prevention, rehabilitation, and patient expectations. This topic is educational and should be interpreted alongside current local pathways and patient-specific assessment.
keyMechanisms: Advanced joint degeneration produces pain, stiffness, and impaired function
arthroplasty may improve pain and mobility in selected patients. Outcomes depend on comorbidity optimisation, infection prevention, rehabilitation, and patient expectations.

title: Elective Hysterectomy for Benign Disease
source_title: Berek & Novak's Gynecology, 17th edition

redFlags: Possible pregnancy or unexplained postmenopausal bleeding
Suspicion of malignancy or rapidly changing mass
Severe anaemia or active infection
Uncontrolled cardiopulmonary disease
symptoms: Evaluate the characteristic symptom pattern of Elective Hysterectomy for Benign Disease, including onset, evolution, severity, associated symptoms, precipitating factors, complications, and relevant negative findings.
Clarify onset, progression, associated symptoms, baseline function, medicines and the patient’s own priorities.
Ask about relevant risk factors and context described in the case; document important negative findings rather than assuming their absence.
physicalSigns: Record observations and a focused examination directed to the organ system and competing diagnoses in this topic.
Assess functional change, comorbidity, hydration/perfusion where relevant, and baseline status.
Use serial reassessment when the condition or treatment can change over hours or days.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: May coexist and influence pain expectations.
Requires appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Consider with lifelong heavy bleeding or family history.

ruleIn.testName: Pelvic examination and ultrasound when indicated
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Pelvic examination and ultrasound when indicated — The structural cause of symptoms and operative anatomy
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Fibroids, adnexal pathology or other pelvic findings influence the indication and approach.
ruleIn.targetCondition: The structural cause of symptoms and operative anatomy
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Confirms that the planned operation addresses the identified problem.

ruleIn.testName: Full blood count and iron assessment when bleeding suggests deficiency
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Full blood count and iron assessment when bleeding suggests deficiency — Anaemia or iron depletion
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Reduced haemoglobin and iron indices support blood-loss-related deficiency.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Enables preoperative optimisation and blood-management planning.

ruleOut.testName: Pregnancy testing with consent when relevant
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Pregnancy testing with consent when relevant — An unrecognised pregnancy
ruleOut.expectedFinding: A positive result changes the operative plan and requires pregnancy-specific assessment.
ruleOut.targetCondition: An unrecognised pregnancy
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Avoids proceeding with an elective intervention before pregnancy status is addressed.

ruleOut.testName: Endometrial sampling when age, bleeding pattern or risk indicates it
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Endometrial sampling when age, bleeding pattern or risk indicates it — Endometrial hyperplasia or malignancy
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Histology identifies disease that may require an oncology rather than benign-surgery pathway.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Endometrial hyperplasia or malignancy
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Excludes an important alternative before finalising treatment and surgical route.

pathophysiology.summary: Hysterectomy removes the uterus and can definitively treat selected benign conditions, but ends fertility and carries operative, urinary, sexual, and recovery implications. Choice of route and alternatives should reflect anatomy, symptoms, risk, and values. This topic is educational and should be interpreted alongside current local pathways and patient-specific assessment.

title: Elective Valve Intervention Assessment
source_title: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd edition

redFlags: Syncope or exertional chest pain with severe stenosis
Pulmonary oedema or decompensated heart failure
Endocarditis concern or embolic event
Rapid decline in ventricular function
symptoms: Evaluate the characteristic symptom pattern of Elective Valve Intervention Assessment, including onset, evolution, severity, associated symptoms, precipitating factors, complications, and relevant negative findings.
Clarify onset, progression, associated symptoms, baseline function, medicines and the patient’s own priorities.
Ask about relevant risk factors and context described in the case; document important negative findings rather than assuming their absence.
physicalSigns: Record observations and a focused examination directed to the organ system and competing diagnoses in this topic.
Assess functional change, comorbidity, hydration/perfusion where relevant, and baseline status.
Use serial reassessment when the condition or treatment can change over hours or days.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: May coexist and contribute to symptoms.
Can explain exercise limitation but does not negate severe valve disease.
Multifactorial symptoms need structured review.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Comprehensive echocardiography — Valve lesion severity and ventricular response
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Valve haemodynamics, chamber size and ventricular function define the lesion in context.
ruleIn.targetCondition: Valve lesion severity and ventricular response
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Establishes severity and supports intervention timing and type.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: ECG and functional assessment — Rhythm disturbance and symptom burden
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Arrhythmia and exertional limitation may indicate clinical consequences of valve disease.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Connects imaging severity with the patient's actual functional state.

ruleOut.testName: Renal, frailty and coronary assessment as indicated
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Renal, frailty and coronary assessment as indicated — Comorbidity affecting procedural benefit or risk
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Organ dysfunction, frailty or coronary disease may alter the Heart Team plan.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Comorbidity affecting procedural benefit or risk
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Supports an individualised procedure and consent rather than anatomy-only selection.

pathophysiology.summary: Valve obstruction or regurgitation changes pressure and volume loading, eventually impairing cardiac output and ventricular function. Intervention timing depends on lesion severity, symptoms, cardiac response, procedural risk, and expected benefit. This topic is educational and should be interpreted alongside current local pathways and patient-specific assessment.
keyMechanisms: Valve obstruction or regurgitation changes pressure and volume loading, eventually impairing cardiac output and ventricular function. Intervention timing depends on lesion severity, symptoms, cardiac response, procedural risk, and expected benefit.

title: Fetal Growth Restriction Assessment
source_title: Gabbe's Obstetrics: Normal and Problem Pregnancies, 9th edition

redFlags: Absent/reversed end-diastolic flow
Reduced fetal movement or non-reassuring testing
Severe maternal hypertension or placental abruption
Growth restriction with major anomaly or infection concern
symptoms: Evaluate the characteristic symptom pattern of Fetal Growth Restriction Assessment, including onset, evolution, severity, associated symptoms, precipitating factors, complications, and relevant negative findings.
Clarify onset, progression, associated symptoms, baseline function, medicines and the patient’s own priorities.
Ask about relevant risk factors and context described in the case; document important negative findings rather than assuming their absence.
physicalSigns: Record observations and a focused examination directed to the organ system and competing diagnoses in this topic.
Assess functional change, comorbidity, hydration/perfusion where relevant, and baseline status.
Use serial reassessment when the condition or treatment can change over hours or days.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Stable growth and normal placental assessment may support this.
Early dating record is important.
Targeted assessment based on findings.

ruleIn.testName: Serial ultrasound biometry with dating review
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Serial ultrasound biometry with dating review — Small fetal size and reduced growth velocity
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Size centiles and serial growth must be interpreted against reliable gestational dating.
ruleIn.targetCondition: Small fetal size and reduced growth velocity
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Distinguishes a small fetus from a concerning growth trajectory.

ruleIn.testName: Umbilical artery Doppler and amniotic-fluid assessment
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Umbilical artery Doppler and amniotic-fluid assessment — Placental resistance and fetal compromise risk
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Abnormal Doppler flow or reduced fluid increases concern for placental dysfunction.
ruleIn.targetCondition: Placental resistance and fetal compromise risk
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Stratifies risk and informs specialist surveillance and delivery planning.

ruleOut.testName: Maternal blood-pressure and pre-eclampsia assessment
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Maternal blood-pressure and pre-eclampsia assessment — Maternal hypertensive disease accompanying placental dysfunction
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Elevated pressure, proteinuria or organ dysfunction requires the obstetric hypertension pathway.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Maternal hypertensive disease accompanying placental dysfunction
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Detects a maternal condition that changes urgency and management for both mother and fetus.

pathophysiology.summary: Placental insufficiency can restrict oxygen and nutrient delivery, altering fetal growth and increasing stillbirth and neonatal risk. Maternal vascular disease, fetal anomalies, infection, and inaccurate dating are important alternatives. This topic is educational and should be interpreted alongside current local pathways and patient-specific assessment.
keyMechanisms: Placental insufficiency can restrict oxygen and nutrient delivery, altering fetal growth and increasing stillbirth and neonatal risk. Maternal vascular disease, fetal anomalies, infection, and inaccurate dating are important alternatives.
Clinical expression and progression vary with baseline risk, comorbidity, treatment exposure, and access to timely care.

title: Heart Failure
source_title: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd edition

redFlags: Syncope, rest dyspnoea, or rapidly increasing oedema
Chest pain or new arrhythmia
Hypotension, cool peripheries, or reduced urine output
New confusion or acute kidney dysfunction
symptoms: Evaluate the characteristic symptom pattern of Heart Failure, including onset, evolution, severity, associated symptoms, precipitating factors, complications, and relevant negative findings.
Clarify onset, progression, associated symptoms, baseline function, medicines and the patient’s own priorities.
Ask about relevant risk factors and context described in the case; document important negative findings rather than assuming their absence.
physicalSigns: Record observations and a focused examination directed to the organ system and competing diagnoses in this topic.
Assess functional change, comorbidity, hydration/perfusion where relevant, and baseline status.
Use serial reassessment when the condition or treatment can change over hours or days.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: May coexist; respiratory phenotype and congestion assessment help separate contributions.
Kidney trajectory and volume status guide attribution.

differentials.condition: Anaemia, thyroid disease, ischaemia, or arrhythmia
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Can mimic or worsen functional decline.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Echocardiography — Ventricular dysfunction or important structural disease
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Reduced ejection fraction, valve disease or relevant diastolic abnormalities help define the phenotype.
ruleIn.targetCondition: Ventricular dysfunction or important structural disease
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Establishes cardiac structure/function and directs phenotype-specific care.

ruleIn.testName: Natriuretic peptide when indicated by the diagnostic pathway
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Natriuretic peptide when indicated by the diagnostic pathway — A biochemical signal of cardiac wall stress
ruleIn.expectedFinding: A raised value supports further assessment but is not specific; renal disease, rhythm and body habitus affect interpretation.
ruleIn.targetCondition: A biochemical signal of cardiac wall stress
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Helps triage diagnostic imaging in suspected heart failure.

ruleOut.testName: Creatinine, electrolytes, full blood count and iron status when indicated
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Creatinine, electrolytes, full blood count and iron status when indicated — Organ dysfunction, electrolyte disturbance and anaemia/iron deficiency
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Abnormal results may contribute to symptoms or limit treatment tolerance.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Organ dysfunction, electrolyte disturbance and anaemia/iron deficiency
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Establishes a monitoring baseline and identifies potentially correctable comorbidity.

ruleOut.testName: 12-lead ECG
ruleOut.modalityTarget: 12-lead ECG — Arrhythmia, conduction disturbance or prior ischaemic disease
ruleOut.expectedFinding: An abnormal rhythm or conduction pattern directs further assessment; ECG alone does not define heart-failure phenotype.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Arrhythmia, conduction disturbance or prior ischaemic disease
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Identifies contributors that can alter treatment or specialist referral.

pathophysiology.summary: Structural or functional cardiac impairment raises filling pressures and/or limits output. Neurohormonal activation and remodelling contribute to progression; phenotype and comorbidity guide treatment choices. This topic is educational and should be interpreted alongside current local pathways and patient-specific assessment.
keyMechanisms: Structural or functional cardiac impairment raises filling pressures and/or limits output. Neurohormonal activation and remodelling contribute to progression
phenotype and comorbidity guide treatment choices.

title: Hyperosmolar Hyperglycaemic State
source_title: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd edition

redFlags: Shock, coma, or seizures
Acute focal neurological deficit
Severe electrolyte abnormality or pulmonary oedema
Inability to protect airway or worsening consciousness
symptoms: Evaluate the characteristic symptom pattern of Hyperosmolar Hyperglycaemic State, including onset, evolution, severity, associated symptoms, precipitating factors, complications, and relevant negative findings.
Clarify onset, progression, associated symptoms, baseline function, medicines and the patient’s own priorities.
Ask about relevant risk factors and context described in the case; document important negative findings rather than assuming their absence.
physicalSigns: Record observations and a focused examination directed to the organ system and competing diagnoses in this topic.
Assess functional change, comorbidity, hydration/perfusion where relevant, and baseline status.
Use serial reassessment when the condition or treatment can change over hours or days.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Ketonaemia and acidosis define a ketoacidotic or overlap component.
Abrupt focal findings require emergency stroke evaluation.
May precipitate HHS and independently alter cognition.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Glucose, electrolytes and measured/calculated osmolality — Severe hyperglycaemia and hyperosmolality
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Marked glucose elevation with raised osmolality supports HHS in the clinical context.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Defines the metabolic disturbance and monitors the trajectory of correction under the local protocol.

ruleIn.testName: Creatinine, urine output and neurological observations
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Creatinine, urine output and neurological observations — Kidney hypoperfusion, dehydration and neurological change
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Renal deterioration, low urine output or altered consciousness indicates significant systemic involvement.
ruleIn.targetCondition: Kidney hypoperfusion, dehydration and neurological change
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Guides individualised fluids and prompts reassessment of neurological deterioration.

ruleOut.testName: Blood ketones and venous blood gas
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Blood ketones and venous blood gas — Significant ketosis/acidosis or overlap with DKA
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Substantial ketonaemia or acidosis suggests mixed DKA/HHS rather than isolated HHS.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Significant ketosis/acidosis or overlap with DKA
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Distinguishes overlapping emergencies that require different treatment monitoring.

ruleOut.testName: ECG and source-directed precipitant investigation
ruleOut.modalityTarget: ECG and source-directed precipitant investigation — Infection, ischaemia or another acute trigger
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Clinical clues select the named tests; abnormalities direct parallel treatment.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Infection, ischaemia or another acute trigger
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Identifies the cause of decompensation without delaying metabolic stabilisation.

pathophysiology.summary: Residual insulin may suppress ketogenesis while failing to prevent severe hyperglycaemia; prolonged osmotic diuresis causes profound water deficit and hyperosmolality. Infection, impaired access to fluids, medicines, and vascular illness are common contributors. This topic is educational and should be interpreted alongside current local pathways and patient-specific assessment.
keyMechanisms: Residual insulin may suppress ketogenesis while failing to prevent severe hyperglycaemia
prolonged osmotic diuresis causes profound water deficit and hyperosmolality. Infection, impaired access to fluids, medicines, and vascular illness are common contributors.

title: Hypertension in Adults [Adapted from NICE]
source_title: NICE NG136: Hypertension in adults — diagnosis and management

content.title: Hypertension in Adults [Adapted from NICE]
content.specialty: Family Medicine, Internal Medicine and Cardiology

redFlags: Blood pressure at or above the severe range with retinal haemorrhage/papilloedema, confusion, chest pain, acute kidney injury or heart failure
Pregnancy or possible pregnancy with severe hypertension or concerning symptoms
Acute focal neurological deficit or aortic-dissection features
Suspected catecholamine crisis or another rapidly progressive secondary cause
symptoms: Usually asymptomatic and detected on screening
Headache or dizziness, which are non-specific
Symptoms of target-organ disease such as exertional chest discomfort, breathlessness or neurological episodes
Features suggesting a secondary cause, including episodic palpitations, muscle weakness or sleep apnoea
physicalSigns: Repeated elevated clinic blood pressure using correct technique
Postural blood-pressure fall in older adults, diabetes or symptomatic patients
Retinal vascular change
Signs of left-ventricular hypertrophy, heart failure, peripheral vascular disease or endocrine disease

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Raised clinic readings with normal validated ambulatory or home averages.
Normal clinic readings but elevated out-of-office averages or unexplained target-organ damage.
Young onset, abrupt worsening, resistant disease, hypokalaemia, renal findings, endocrine features or a medicine/substance trigger.
Pain, anxiety, acute illness or recent stimulant exposure with normal readings after the driver resolves.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Standardised repeated clinic blood pressure — Persistent clinic hypertension
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Clinic blood pressure remains at or above the diagnostic threshold after repeat measurement with correct cuff and positioning.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Technique and repetition reduce random error and identify inter-arm difference.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Ambulatory blood-pressure monitoring — Sustained hypertension
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Average waking readings meet the validated diagnostic threshold using adequate measurements.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Preferred confirmation method for clinic readings below the severe range and distinguishes white-coat effect.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Home blood-pressure monitoring — Sustained hypertension when ABPM is unsuitable
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Average readings after discarding the first day meet the validated home threshold.
ruleIn.targetCondition: Sustained hypertension when ABPM is unsuitable
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Provides confirmation and supports later self-monitoring when performed with a validated device and protocol.

ruleOut.testName: Urine albumin-creatinine ratio and urinalysis
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Urine albumin-creatinine ratio and urinalysis — Chronic kidney disease or renal target-organ damage
ruleOut.expectedFinding: No albuminuria or haematuria, or an abnormality prompts renal evaluation.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Chronic kidney disease or renal target-organ damage
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Renal disease can be both a cause and consequence of hypertension and changes treatment choice and targets.

ruleOut.testName: Electrolytes, creatinine/eGFR, glycated haemoglobin and lipid profile
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Electrolytes, creatinine/eGFR, glycated haemoglobin and lipid profile — Secondary contributor and cardiovascular comorbidity
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Baseline metabolic and renal status is defined; hypokalaemia, kidney dysfunction or diabetes redirects assessment.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Secondary contributor and cardiovascular comorbidity
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Supports cardiovascular-risk estimation and safe medicine selection.

ruleOut.testName: Fundoscopy and 12-lead electrocardiogram
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Fundoscopy and 12-lead electrocardiogram — Retinal or cardiac target-organ damage
ruleOut.expectedFinding: No hypertensive retinopathy or left-ventricular/cardiac abnormality, or damage is documented for risk management.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Retinal or cardiac target-organ damage
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Target-organ damage changes urgency and the balance of treatment benefit.

pathophysiology.summary: Sustained arterial hypertension reflects increased systemic vascular resistance, altered sodium-volume balance and neurohormonal activation interacting with age, genetics, adiposity and environmental exposures. Chronic pressure load accelerates vascular remodelling and damages the heart, brain, kidneys, retina and peripheral arteries.
keyMechanisms: Renin-angiotensin-aldosterone and sympathetic activation increase vascular tone and sodium retention.
Endothelial dysfunction and arterial stiffness raise systolic pressure and pulse pressure.
Renal sodium handling and pressure natriuresis reset at a higher arterial pressure.
Persistent load causes left-ventricular hypertrophy, albuminuria, retinopathy and cerebrovascular injury.

clinicalManagement.title: Measure and confirm
actions: Use a validated, maintained device, correct cuff size, supported arm and a quiet seated setting.
Measure both arms initially and use the arm with the persistently higher reading.
Confirm clinic hypertension with ambulatory monitoring or, when unsuitable, structured home monitoring unless urgent severe hypertension requires immediate assessment.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: At initial and confirmation visits

clinicalManagement.title: Identify severe hypertension requiring urgent assessment
actions: Assess for retinal, neurological, cardiac, aortic and renal target-organ injury.
Use emergency transfer for life-threatening symptoms or suspected acute organ injury.
Do not rapidly lower asymptomatic blood pressure outside a monitored, indication-specific protocol.
Activate emergency specialist management and monitored intravenous therapy under the local protocol.
branches.condition: Severe blood pressure with acute target-organ injury

actions: Arrange urgent clinical review, confirm adherence and complete prompt organ assessment rather than routine follow-up.
branches.condition: Severe blood pressure without acute target-organ injury

clinicalManagement.timeframe: Same day when severe readings or symptoms are present

clinicalManagement.title: Assess cardiovascular risk and organ damage
actions: Obtain urine albumin-creatinine ratio, haematuria screen, glycated haemoglobin, electrolytes, creatinine/eGFR and lipids.
Perform fundoscopy and a 12-lead electrocardiogram.
Use a cardiovascular-risk tool validated or approved for local Saudi practice and assess for secondary-cause clues.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: During diagnostic confirmation

clinicalManagement.title: Start lifestyle and pharmacological treatment
actions: Offer lifestyle intervention to every patient and discuss medicine using age, diabetes, kidney disease, pregnancy potential, frailty and cardiovascular risk.
Use generic ACE inhibitors, angiotensin-receptor blockers, calcium-channel blockers or thiazide-like diuretics in the guideline sequence when suitable and SFDA authorised.
Do not combine an ACE inhibitor with an angiotensin-receptor blocker.
Use current SFDA labelling and the local formulary for dose, contraindication and monitoring decisions; this record is not a prescribing source.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: After confirmed diagnosis, sooner when severity or organ damage requires

clinicalManagement.title: Titrate and monitor
actions: Check adherence, side effects, postural symptoms and validated clinic or home readings before intensification.
Monitor kidney function and electrolytes after renin-angiotensin system blockers, diuretics or mineralocorticoid-receptor antagonists according to protocol.
Before labelling resistant hypertension, confirm out-of-office elevation, optimal tolerated triple therapy and adherence, then seek specialist input or use protocol-directed fourth-line treatment.
Individualise targets for frailty, multimorbidity and significant postural hypotension.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: At defined intervals after each treatment change and at least annually once stable

nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Review after initiation or each medicine change until a stable target is achieved, then provide at least annual review of blood pressure, postural symptoms, lifestyle, adherence, adverse effects, renal function and evolving cardiovascular risk.
mdtReferrals: Primary-care pharmacist or nurse for adherence and home-monitoring support
Nephrology, endocrinology or hypertension specialist for suspected secondary or resistant hypertension
Obstetric medicine for pregnancy, pregnancy planning or postpartum hypertension
Dietitian, weight-management and smoking-cessation services according to need
lifestyleAndDiet: Reduce dietary sodium using culturally relevant food choices; avoid potassium-containing salt substitutes when kidney disease, diabetes or interacting medicines make them unsafe.
Encourage regular aerobic and strengthening activity and gradual weight reduction when indicated.
Limit excessive caffeine and alcohol, stop smoking and address sleep apnoea risk.
Do not recommend calcium, magnesium or potassium supplements solely to lower blood pressure.
patientEducation: Explain that hypertension is often silent but treatment reduces long-term cardiovascular and renal risk.
Teach validated home-monitoring technique and how to record readings without excessive repeated checking.
Discuss medicine purpose, common adverse effects, pregnancy precautions and when to seek urgent care.

title: Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy
source_title: Gabbe's Obstetrics: Normal and Problem Pregnancies, 9th edition

redFlags: Severe-range pressure or neurological symptoms
Right upper abdominal pain, dyspnoea, or visual disturbance
Seizure, pulmonary oedema, or reduced fetal movement
Thrombocytopenia, liver injury, or renal deterioration

physicalSigns: Record observations and a focused examination directed to the organ system and competing diagnoses in this topic.
Assess functional change, comorbidity, hydration/perfusion where relevant, and baseline status.
Use serial reassessment when the condition or treatment can change over hours or days.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Pre-pregnancy history and baseline testing help classify.
No proteinuria/severe feature at assessment, but progression risk remains.
Do not attribute new severe headache to benign cause without assessment.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Repeated standardised blood-pressure measurement — Persistent or severe pregnancy-associated hypertension
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Repeated elevated readings require interpretation with gestation, symptoms and prior pressure.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Confirms the measurement and determines urgency using the pregnancy-specific pathway.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Urine protein assessment — Proteinuria accompanying possible pre-eclampsia
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Increased protein supports renal involvement; its absence does not exclude pre-eclampsia with other organ dysfunction.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Contributes to diagnosis without allowing a negative result to dismiss concerning maternal findings.

ruleOut.testName: Full blood count/platelets, creatinine and liver tests
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Full blood count/platelets, creatinine and liver tests — Thrombocytopenia and renal/hepatic organ involvement
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Falling platelets, rising creatinine or transaminases raises concern for severe disease or HELLP-spectrum complications.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Thrombocytopenia and renal/hepatic organ involvement
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Detects organ dysfunction that changes monitoring, escalation and delivery planning.

ruleOut.testName: Fetal growth ultrasound and wellbeing assessment when indicated
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Fetal growth ultrasound and wellbeing assessment when indicated — Placental dysfunction and fetal compromise
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Growth restriction or abnormal surveillance findings influence obstetric decisions.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Placental dysfunction and fetal compromise
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Assesses fetal consequences alongside maternal severity.

pathophysiology.summary: Abnormal placentation and maternal endothelial dysfunction can produce systemic vasoconstriction and organ injury. Disease may progress rapidly, affecting maternal brain, liver, kidney, lungs, coagulation, placenta, and fetus. This topic is educational and should be interpreted alongside current local pathways and patient-specific assessment.

title: Hypothyroidism
source_title: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd edition

redFlags: Altered consciousness, hypothermia, or haemodynamic instability
Pregnancy with untreated or poorly controlled disease
Possible pituitary disorder or adrenal insufficiency
Persistent symptoms despite biochemical normalisation

Clarify onset, progression, associated symptoms, baseline function, medicines and the patient’s own priorities.

physicalSigns: Record observations and a focused examination directed to the organ system and competing diagnoses in this topic.
Assess functional change, comorbidity, hydration/perfusion where relevant, and baseline status.
Use serial reassessment when the condition or treatment can change over hours or days.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Common alternative contributors to fatigue.
May coexist and needs direct assessment.
Pituitary history or discordant TSH/free hormone pattern prompts specialist evaluation.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: TSH and free thyroxine — Primary or central thyroid hormone deficiency
ruleIn.expectedFinding: High TSH with low free thyroxine supports primary disease; low free thyroxine without appropriately raised TSH suggests a central cause.
ruleIn.targetCondition: Primary or central thyroid hormone deficiency

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Thyroid peroxidase antibodies when indicated — Autoimmune thyroid disease
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Positive antibodies support an autoimmune cause but do not measure current thyroid function.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Clarifies aetiology when it changes counselling or follow-up.

ruleOut.testName: Medication, supplement and pituitary assessment when results are discordant
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Medication, supplement and pituitary assessment when results are discordant — Assay interference, drug effects or pituitary disease
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Biotin exposure, relevant medicines or pituitary symptoms may explain a misleading biochemical pattern.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Assay interference, drug effects or pituitary disease
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Avoids incorrect diagnosis and directs repeat or specialist testing.

pathophysiology.summary: Reduced thyroid hormone action slows metabolic processes and can affect cardiovascular, gastrointestinal, neurological, reproductive, and lipid systems. Symptoms are nonspecific; laboratory pattern, medication exposure, pregnancy, and pituitary context shape interpretation. This topic is educational and should be interpreted alongside current local pathways and patient-specific assessment.
keyMechanisms: Reduced thyroid hormone action slows metabolic processes and can affect cardiovascular, gastrointestinal, neurological, reproductive, and lipid systems. Symptoms are nonspecific
laboratory pattern, medication exposure, pregnancy, and pituitary context shape interpretation.

title: Intrapartum Fetal Compromise
source_title: Gabbe's Obstetrics: Normal and Problem Pregnancies, 9th edition

redFlags: Prolonged bradycardia or persistent pathological tracing
Maternal hypotension, haemorrhage, or uterine rupture concern
Tachysystole with fetal changes
Failure to improve despite corrective measures
symptoms: Evaluate the characteristic symptom pattern of Intrapartum Fetal Compromise, including onset, evolution, severity, associated symptoms, precipitating factors, complications, and relevant negative findings.
Clarify onset, progression, associated symptoms, baseline function, medicines and the patient’s own priorities.
Ask about relevant risk factors and context described in the case; document important negative findings rather than assuming their absence.
physicalSigns: Record observations and a focused examination directed to the organ system and competing diagnoses in this topic.
Assess functional change, comorbidity, hydration/perfusion where relevant, and baseline status.
Use serial reassessment when the condition or treatment can change over hours or days.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: May cause fetal tachycardia and compromise.
Can alter variability but context and duration matter.
Confirm fetal rather than maternal heart rate.

ruleIn.testName: Continuous fetal heart-rate monitoring with contraction assessment
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Continuous fetal heart-rate monitoring with contraction assessment — A fetal heart-rate pattern suggesting hypoxia
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Baseline, variability, decelerations and contraction frequency are interpreted together using the locally adopted classification.
ruleIn.targetCondition: A fetal heart-rate pattern suggesting hypoxia
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Detects a concerning trend and guides prompt obstetric escalation; a trace is not interpreted in isolation.

ruleOut.testName: Maternal observations and focused labour assessment
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Maternal observations and focused labour assessment — Maternal hypotension, fever, excessive uterine activity or an obstetric emergency
ruleOut.expectedFinding: A new maternal abnormality or examination finding can explain the fetal pattern and alter urgency.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Maternal hypotension, fever, excessive uterine activity or an obstetric emergency
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Identifies reversible contributors or emergencies while the fetal trace is reassessed.

pathophysiology.summary: Reduced uteroplacental oxygen transfer or cord compression can produce fetal heart-rate changes. Interpretation depends on baseline, variability, decelerations, contractions, maternal condition, and trend rather than a single feature. This topic is educational and should be interpreted alongside current local pathways and patient-specific assessment.
keyMechanisms: Reduced uteroplacental oxygen transfer or cord compression can produce fetal heart-rate changes. Interpretation depends on baseline, variability, decelerations, contractions, maternal condition, and trend rather than a single feature.
Clinical expression and progression vary with baseline risk, comorbidity, treatment exposure, and access to timely care.

title: Ischaemic Heart Disease
source_title: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd edition

redFlags: New rest pain or crescendo symptoms
Syncope, acute dyspnoea, or haemodynamic instability
New neurological deficit
Persistent symptoms despite treatment
symptoms: Evaluate the characteristic symptom pattern of Ischaemic Heart Disease, including onset, evolution, severity, associated symptoms, precipitating factors, complications, and relevant negative findings.
Clarify onset, progression, associated symptoms, baseline function, medicines and the patient’s own priorities.
Ask about relevant risk factors and context described in the case; document important negative findings rather than assuming their absence.
physicalSigns: Record observations and a focused examination directed to the organ system and competing diagnoses in this topic.
Assess functional change, comorbidity, hydration/perfusion where relevant, and baseline status.
Use serial reassessment when the condition or treatment can change over hours or days.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Meal/position relation may help but does not exclude cardiac cause.
Reproducibility may support another cause but is not definitive.
May coexist; assess risk and objective findings.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: 12-lead ECG — Ischaemic change, prior infarction or arrhythmia
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Resting abnormalities may support cardiac disease; a normal ECG does not exclude coronary disease.
ruleIn.targetCondition: Ischaemic change, prior infarction or arrhythmia
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Provides a baseline and identifies findings needing an acute or rhythm-specific pathway.

ruleIn.testName: Risk-selected coronary anatomical or functional testing
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Risk-selected coronary anatomical or functional testing — Obstructive coronary disease or inducible ischaemia
ruleIn.expectedFinding: The selected study identifies anatomy or functional ischaemia in the appropriate pre-test-risk context.
ruleIn.targetCondition: Obstructive coronary disease or inducible ischaemia
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Clarifies uncertain symptoms and directs management; choose the test through the current cardiology pathway.

ruleOut.testName: Lipids, glycaemia and creatinine
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Lipids, glycaemia and creatinine — Modifiable vascular risk and kidney impairment
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Abnormal lipid/glucose measures or renal dysfunction affects prevention and medicine/procedure safety.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Modifiable vascular risk and kidney impairment
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Defines risk-reduction priorities and a baseline for safe care.

pathophysiology.summary: Atherosclerotic plaque and endothelial dysfunction limit coronary flow. Plaque disruption can cause acute thrombosis and myocardial injury; secondary prevention reduces future vascular events. This topic is educational and should be interpreted alongside current local pathways and patient-specific assessment.

secondary prevention reduces future vascular events.

title: Kidney Failure Planning and Dialysis Access
source_title: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd edition

content.title: Kidney Failure Planning and Dialysis Access

redFlags: Rapid decline or refractory metabolic/fluid complication
Acute uraemic symptoms or pericarditis
Access infection, thrombosis, or limb ischaemia
Severe distress or decisional conflict
symptoms: Evaluate the characteristic symptom pattern of Kidney Failure Planning and Dialysis Access, including onset, evolution, severity, associated symptoms, precipitating factors, complications, and relevant negative findings.
Clarify onset, progression, associated symptoms, baseline function, medicines and the patient’s own priorities.
Ask about relevant risk factors and context described in the case; document important negative findings rather than assuming their absence.
physicalSigns: Record observations and a focused examination directed to the organ system and competing diagnoses in this topic.
Assess functional change, comorbidity, hydration/perfusion where relevant, and baseline status.
Use serial reassessment when the condition or treatment can change over hours or days.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Abrupt decline may be reversible and alter timing.
May be treatable before irreversible progression.
A valid active pathway, not absence of care.

ruleIn.testName: Serial eGFR, albuminuria and kidney-failure-risk assessment
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Serial eGFR, albuminuria and kidney-failure-risk assessment — Progression and likelihood of kidney failure
ruleIn.expectedFinding: The trend and validated risk estimate inform planning; one eGFR value alone does not determine dialysis initiation.
ruleIn.targetCondition: Progression and likelihood of kidney failure
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Allows timely modality, access and transplant discussion according to trajectory and patient preference.

ruleIn.testName: Potassium, bicarbonate, haemoglobin and mineral-bone profile when indicated
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Potassium, bicarbonate, haemoglobin and mineral-bone profile when indicated — Complications of advanced kidney disease
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Electrolyte, acid-base, anaemia or mineral abnormalities require individualised management.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Identifies complications that affect urgency and readiness for renal replacement options.

ruleOut.testName: Vascular mapping when haemodialysis access is planned
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Vascular mapping when haemodialysis access is planned — Suitable arteries and veins for access
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Vessel size, patency and anatomy guide the access team's choice.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Suitable arteries and veins for access
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Supports access planning rather than automatic fistula creation irrespective of goals or modality.

pathophysiology.summary: Progressive nephron loss may lead to fluid, electrolyte, and uraemic complications. Preparation before kidney failure allows informed modality choice and planned access; the best pathway depends on health, support, geography, and preferences. This topic is educational and should be interpreted alongside current local pathways and patient-specific assessment.
keyMechanisms: Progressive nephron loss may lead to fluid, electrolyte, and uraemic complications. Preparation before kidney failure allows informed modality choice and planned access
the best pathway depends on health, support, geography, and preferences.

title: Last Days of Life Care
source_title: Oxford Textbook of Palliative Medicine, 6th edition

redFlags: Uncontrolled pain, dyspnoea, seizure, or major bleeding
Potentially reversible cause consistent with expressed goals
Medication toxicity or distressing secretions
Family distress, conflict, or lack of support
symptoms: Evaluate the characteristic symptom pattern of Last Days of Life Care, including onset, evolution, severity, associated symptoms, precipitating factors, complications, and relevant negative findings.
Clarify onset, progression, associated symptoms, baseline function, medicines and the patient’s own priorities.
Ask about relevant risk factors and context described in the case; document important negative findings rather than assuming their absence.
physicalSigns: Record observations and a focused examination directed to the organ system and competing diagnoses in this topic.
Assess functional change, comorbidity, hydration/perfusion where relevant, and baseline status.
Use serial reassessment when the condition or treatment can change over hours or days.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Assess reversible causes proportionately.
Review recent changes and renal function.
May contribute but does not alone establish dying.

ruleIn.testName: Clinical trajectory and repeated symptom assessment
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Clinical trajectory and repeated symptom assessment — Dying-phase changes and distress
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Progressive decline, altered consciousness and symptom burden are interpreted with the whole clinical trajectory.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Supports recognition, communication and comfort planning while acknowledging uncertainty.

ruleOut.testName: Focused review for a reversible source of distress
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Focused review for a reversible source of distress — Pain, retention, constipation or medication-related harm
ruleOut.expectedFinding: A specific contributor may be identified by examination and medication review.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Pain, retention, constipation or medication-related harm
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Offers proportionate relief; laboratory or imaging tests should be added only if they change goal-concordant care.

pathophysiology.summary: Physiological decline near death may involve reduced intake, consciousness, mobility, and organ function. These changes can be distressing but vary; clear communication and repeated symptom review support comfort and family understanding. This topic is educational and should be interpreted alongside current local pathways and patient-specific assessment.

title: Lung Cancer Management
source_title: Saudi Lung Cancer Management Guidelines

content.title: Lung Cancer Management
content.specialty: Thoracic Oncology, Respiratory Medicine and Thoracic Surgery

redFlags: Massive haemoptysis or threatened airway
Superior vena cava obstruction with respiratory or neurological compromise
Spinal-cord compression symptoms or new focal neurological deficit
Severe hypercalcaemia, pericardial tamponade or rapidly worsening respiratory failure
symptoms: Persistent or changing cough
Haemoptysis, breathlessness or chest pain
Unexplained weight loss, fatigue or recurrent focal pneumonia
Hoarseness, bone pain, headache or focal neurological symptoms
physicalSigns: Focal reduced air entry, wheeze or signs of pleural effusion
Supraclavicular lymphadenopathy
Clubbing or features of superior vena cava obstruction
Neurological deficit, bony tenderness or paraneoplastic manifestations

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Epidemiologic risk, constitutional symptoms, cavitation and specific microbiological evidence.
Acute infective presentation that resolves radiographically; persistence or recurrence in one lobe raises concern for obstruction.
Stable interval imaging or benign calcification/morphology within a validated nodule pathway.
Known extrathoracic cancer and pathology/immunophenotype inconsistent with a pulmonary primary.

ruleIn.testName: Contrast-enhanced CT chest and upper abdomen
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Contrast-enhanced CT chest and upper abdomen — Primary lung malignancy and anatomical stage
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Suspicious pulmonary lesion with local, nodal or metastatic features.
ruleIn.targetCondition: Primary lung malignancy and anatomical stage
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Defines the safest highest-yield biopsy target and initial resectability assessment.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Image-guided, bronchoscopic or endobronchial-ultrasound biopsy — Histological lung-cancer diagnosis
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Adequate tissue confirms histology and supports molecular and immune biomarker testing.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Tissue method should maximise diagnostic and staging value while minimising procedural risk.

ruleIn.testName: PET-CT and brain imaging when stage appropriate
ruleIn.modalityTarget: PET-CT and brain imaging when stage appropriate — Occult nodal or distant metastasis
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Metabolically or anatomically suspicious disease requiring confirmation when it changes curative intent.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Prevents futile local treatment and guides invasive staging.

ruleOut.testName: Microbiology on appropriate respiratory specimens
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Microbiology on appropriate respiratory specimens — Tuberculosis or fungal infection
ruleOut.expectedFinding: No microbiological evidence of an infectious mimic, or infection is identified for treatment and isolation measures.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Tuberculosis or fungal infection
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Infection can mimic malignancy and is especially important in cavitary disease.

ruleOut.testName: Interval nodule imaging within a validated pathway
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Interval nodule imaging within a validated pathway — Benign or indolent pulmonary nodule
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Long-term stability or benign evolution lowers malignancy probability.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Benign or indolent pulmonary nodule
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Avoids invasive testing for appropriately selected low-risk nodules while preserving surveillance safety.

pathophysiology.summary: Lung cancer arises from malignant transformation of respiratory epithelium and is broadly classified as non-small-cell or small-cell carcinoma. Local invasion, lymphatic spread and early haematogenous dissemination determine resectability and systemic treatment; molecular drivers and immune phenotype increasingly guide therapy.
keyMechanisms: Tobacco smoke, environmental and occupational carcinogens produce cumulative genomic injury.
Histological subtype and molecular alterations determine growth pattern and treatment sensitivity.
Mediastinal nodal involvement strongly affects stage and curative options.
Metastatic spread commonly affects brain, bone, liver and adrenal glands; paraneoplastic syndromes may precede local symptoms.

clinicalManagement.title: Obtain diagnosis and full stage
actions: Choose a biopsy that provides diagnosis and the greatest staging information with acceptable risk.
Complete TNM staging and document performance status, pulmonary function and comorbidity.
Obtain adequate tissue for current molecular-driver and immune biomarker testing in eligible non-small-cell disease.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Urgently after suspicious imaging

clinicalManagement.title: Agree treatment in thoracic MDT
actions: Include respiratory medicine, thoracic surgery, medical oncology, radiation oncology, radiology, pathology and supportive care.
State whether intent is curative, disease controlling or symptom focused.
Discuss clinical trials and the patient's informed preferences.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: After staging and biomarker work-up

clinicalManagement.title: Treat localised disease
actions: Offer anatomical surgical resection with nodal evaluation to operable patients when oncologically appropriate.
Use definitive stereotactic or conventional radiotherapy for selected medically inoperable localised disease.
Consider peri-operative systemic therapy according to stage, histology, biomarkers and the current protocol.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Without avoidable delay

clinicalManagement.title: Treat locally advanced disease
actions: Assess suitability for combined-modality chemoradiotherapy or selected surgical pathways.
Use generic systemic agents and radiotherapy schedules only from the current approved oncology protocol.
Monitor pulmonary, oesophageal, haematological and immune-related toxicity.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: According to MDT sequence

clinicalManagement.title: Treat advanced disease and complications
actions: Select targeted therapy, immunotherapy or cytotoxic chemotherapy according to histology, molecular findings, immune phenotype and fitness.
Use palliative radiotherapy, pleural procedures, analgesia and other symptom-directed interventions early.
Escalate cord compression, major haemoptysis, severe hypercalcaemia and superior vena cava obstruction through emergency oncology pathways.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Promptly after biomarker results; immediately for oncological emergencies

nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Use stage- and treatment-specific surveillance with symptom review and scheduled imaging under the thoracic MDT; monitor late pulmonary and treatment effects and re-biopsy or repeat molecular assessment when progression could alter therapy.
mdtReferrals: Thoracic surgery, medical oncology, radiation oncology and respiratory medicine
Molecular pathology/genomics for eligible disease
Palliative care from diagnosis of advanced disease or high symptom burden
Dietitian, physiotherapy, psycho-oncology and smoking-cessation service
lifestyleAndDiet: Provide evidence-based tobacco-cessation treatment at every stage without making treatment conditional on cessation.
Assess weight loss and sarcopenia and provide early nutrition support.
Encourage pulmonary rehabilitation or activity adapted to symptoms and treatment.
patientEducation: Explain histology, stage, biomarker results, treatment intent and realistic benefits and harms.
Provide urgent warning signs for haemoptysis, neurological change, cord compression and treatment toxicity.
Offer shared decision support that includes supportive-care-only options when appropriate.
dischargeCriteria: Diagnosis, stage, biomarkers and MDT treatment intent are documented.
Acute respiratory or metabolic complications are controlled.
The patient has named contacts, toxicity guidance and a scheduled treatment or surveillance visit.

title: Malignant Bowel Obstruction Support
source_title: Oxford Textbook of Palliative Medicine, 6th edition

redFlags: Peritonitis, perforation, or sepsis
Uncontrolled vomiting or severe dehydration
Ischaemia or rapidly worsening pain
Inability to manage symptoms in current setting
symptoms: Evaluate the characteristic symptom pattern of Malignant Bowel Obstruction Support, including onset, evolution, severity, associated symptoms, precipitating factors, complications, and relevant negative findings.
Clarify onset, progression, associated symptoms, baseline function, medicines and the patient’s own priorities.
Ask about relevant risk factors and context described in the case; document important negative findings rather than assuming their absence.
physicalSigns: Record observations and a focused examination directed to the organ system and competing diagnoses in this topic.
Assess functional change, comorbidity, hydration/perfusion where relevant, and baseline status.
Use serial reassessment when the condition or treatment can change over hours or days.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: May mimic or contribute to obstruction.
Review opioids and anticholinergic burden.
Can coexist and may be reversible.

ruleIn.testName: Abdominal examination, bowel history and medication review
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Abdominal examination, bowel history and medication review — Obstruction pattern, symptom burden and contributing constipation
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Vomiting, distension, reduced stool/flatus and medication effects guide the working assessment.
ruleIn.targetCondition: Obstruction pattern, symptom burden and contributing constipation
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Identifies the dominant symptoms and potentially reversible contributors before choosing an intervention.

ruleIn.testName: CT abdomen/pelvis when results will alter management
ruleIn.modalityTarget: CT abdomen/pelvis when results will alter management — Obstruction site, extent and procedural options
ruleIn.expectedFinding: A transition point, multifocal disease or a complication affects surgical, endoscopic or decompressive choices.
ruleIn.targetCondition: Obstruction site, extent and procedural options
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Clarifies whether an intervention is feasible and consistent with the patient's goals.

ruleOut.testName: Creatinine and electrolytes when clinically useful
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Creatinine and electrolytes when clinically useful — Dehydration and metabolic disturbance
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Renal impairment or electrolyte losses may accompany vomiting and poor intake.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Dehydration and metabolic disturbance
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Guides proportionate fluids and symptom-medicine safety.

pathophysiology.summary: Tumour infiltration, adhesions, dysmotility, or extrinsic compression can impede bowel transit. Obstruction may be partial or complete and cause pain, vomiting, fluid loss, and distress; management should reflect anatomy and goals. This topic is educational and should be interpreted alongside current local pathways and patient-specific assessment.
keyMechanisms: Tumour infiltration, adhesions, dysmotility, or extrinsic compression can impede bowel transit. Obstruction may be partial or complete and cause pain, vomiting, fluid loss, and distress
management should reflect anatomy and goals.

title: Maternal Sepsis in Pregnancy or Postpartum
source_title: Gabbe's Obstetrics: Normal and Problem Pregnancies, 9th edition

content.title: Maternal Sepsis in Pregnancy or Postpartum

redFlags: Hypotension, altered mental state, oliguria, or rising lactate
Respiratory compromise
Suspected necrotising infection or retained products
Rapid deterioration or fetal compromise
symptoms: Evaluate the characteristic symptom pattern of Maternal Sepsis in Pregnancy or Postpartum, including onset, evolution, severity, associated symptoms, precipitating factors, complications, and relevant negative findings.
Clarify onset, progression, associated symptoms, baseline function, medicines and the patient’s own priorities.
Ask about relevant risk factors and context described in the case; document important negative findings rather than assuming their absence.
physicalSigns: Record observations and a focused examination directed to the organ system and competing diagnoses in this topic.
Assess functional change, comorbidity, hydration/perfusion where relevant, and baseline status.
Use serial reassessment when the condition or treatment can change over hours or days.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Expected changes do not explain progressive systemic instability.
Uterine tenderness/discharge and obstetric history support source evaluation.
Search beyond the genital tract.

ruleIn.testName: Blood cultures and source cultures when indicated
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Blood cultures and source cultures when indicated — The causative organism
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Growth and susceptibility results help target therapy; negative cultures do not exclude sepsis.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Supports antimicrobial narrowing; collection must not cause a meaningful delay to urgent treatment.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Lactate and renal/liver/coagulation profile — Hypoperfusion and organ dysfunction
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Raised lactate or deteriorating organ indices increases concern; a normal lactate does not exclude maternal sepsis.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Assesses severity and response alongside maternal observations and the current sepsis bundle.

ruleOut.testName: Source-directed ultrasound or other imaging
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Source-directed ultrasound or other imaging — Retained infected tissue, a collection or another treatable focus
ruleOut.expectedFinding: A localised focus may require drainage, evacuation or another source-control intervention.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Retained infected tissue, a collection or another treatable focus
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Selects the appropriate source-control plan with obstetric and relevant specialist teams.

pathophysiology.summary: Infection triggers dysregulated host response, endothelial injury, vasodilation, and organ dysfunction. Pregnancy and postpartum changes may mask early signs, and source control is as important as antimicrobial treatment. This topic is educational and should be interpreted alongside current local pathways and patient-specific assessment.
keyMechanisms: Infection triggers dysregulated host response, endothelial injury, vasodilation, and organ dysfunction. Pregnancy and postpartum changes may mask early signs, and source control is as important as antimicrobial treatment.
Clinical expression and progression vary with baseline risk, comorbidity, treatment exposure, and access to timely care.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Fracture-risk, falls and medication assessment — Fragility fracture history and future fracture risk
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Prior low-trauma fractures, fall risk and relevant exposures inform the locally adopted risk estimate.

ruleOut.modalityTarget: Targeted calcium, renal, vitamin D or other cause-specific tests — A secondary cause or factor affecting treatment safety
