title: Postpartum Haemorrhage Response
source_title: Gabbe's Obstetrics: Normal and Problem Pregnancies, 9th edition

redFlags: Ongoing heavy bleeding or shock
Altered consciousness or collapse
Coagulopathy or rapidly falling haemoglobin
Suspected uterine rupture or retained placenta
symptoms: Evaluate the characteristic symptom pattern of Postpartum Haemorrhage Response, including onset, evolution, severity, associated symptoms, precipitating factors, complications, and relevant negative findings.
Clarify onset, progression, associated symptoms, baseline function, medicines and the patient’s own priorities.
Ask about relevant risk factors and context described in the case; document important negative findings rather than assuming their absence.
physicalSigns: Record observations and a focused examination directed to the organ system and competing diagnoses in this topic.
Assess functional change, comorbidity, hydration/perfusion where relevant, and baseline status.
Use serial reassessment when the condition or treatment can change over hours or days.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Inspect for lacerations when appropriate.
Assess placenta and uterine cavity per protocol.
Rare but time-critical alternate mechanisms.

ruleIn.testName: Quantified blood loss and serial maternal observations
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Quantified blood loss and serial maternal observations — Ongoing haemorrhage and circulatory compromise
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Continuing blood loss, tachycardia or falling pressure raises concern; physiological change may lag behind bleeding.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Tracks severity and response while resuscitation and cause control proceed.

ruleIn.testName: Full blood count, coagulation and fibrinogen
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Full blood count, coagulation and fibrinogen — Anaemia, platelet deficiency and coagulopathy
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Falling haemoglobin/platelets or abnormal coagulation/fibrinogen informs blood-product assessment; early haemoglobin can be misleading.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Guides the haemorrhage/transfusion pathway without delaying immediate treatment.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Blood group and crossmatch — Compatible blood products
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Compatibility testing enables appropriate transfusion support.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Prepares urgently needed products through the local major-haemorrhage protocol.

ruleOut.testName: Focused obstetric examination with ultrasound when useful
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Focused obstetric examination with ultrasound when useful — Atony, trauma, retained tissue or another bleeding cause
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Uterine tone, genital trauma or retained tissue directs cause-specific intervention.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Atony, trauma, retained tissue or another bleeding cause
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Identifies the source; imaging must not delay action for clinically evident haemorrhage.

pathophysiology.summary: Postpartum haemorrhage results from impaired uterine contraction, genital tract trauma, retained tissue, or coagulation failure. Blood loss can outpace visible estimation and lead to shock, coagulopathy, and organ injury. This topic is educational and should be interpreted alongside current local pathways and patient-specific assessment.
keyMechanisms: Postpartum haemorrhage results from impaired uterine contraction, genital tract trauma, retained tissue, or coagulation failure. Blood loss can outpace visible estimation and lead to shock, coagulopathy, and organ injury.
Clinical expression and progression vary with baseline risk, comorbidity, treatment exposure, and access to timely care.

title: Preconception Health and Risk Review
source_title: Gabbe's Obstetrics: Normal and Problem Pregnancies, 9th edition

redFlags: Current pregnancy with high-risk medicine exposure
Poorly controlled diabetes, seizures, hypertension, or cardiac disease
Medication change that could destabilise serious illness
Intimate partner violence or safeguarding concern
symptoms: Evaluate the characteristic symptom pattern of Preconception Health and Risk Review, including onset, evolution, severity, associated symptoms, precipitating factors, complications, and relevant negative findings.
Clarify onset, progression, associated symptoms, baseline function, medicines and the patient’s own priorities.
Ask about relevant risk factors and context described in the case; document important negative findings rather than assuming their absence.
physicalSigns: Record observations and a focused examination directed to the organ system and competing diagnoses in this topic.
Assess functional change, comorbidity, hydration/perfusion where relevant, and baseline status.
Use serial reassessment when the condition or treatment can change over hours or days.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Different pathway if conception has not occurred after appropriate interval.
Needs timely, nonjudgemental medication and risk review.
Do not stop essential therapy abruptly without prescriber review.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Disease-control and medication review — Maternal conditions or medicines that may affect pregnancy
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Suboptimal disease control or potentially harmful exposures require an individualised plan.
ruleIn.targetCondition: Maternal conditions or medicines that may affect pregnancy
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Allows safer pregnancy preparation and specialist input before conception.

ruleIn.testName: Blood pressure and risk-selected glycaemia assessment
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Blood pressure and risk-selected glycaemia assessment — Unrecognised or poorly controlled cardiometabolic disease
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Elevated pressure or glycaemia requires confirmation and optimisation.
ruleIn.targetCondition: Unrecognised or poorly controlled cardiometabolic disease
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Identifies modifiable maternal risk before pregnancy.

ruleOut.testName: Pregnancy test when clinically relevant and with consent
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Pregnancy test when clinically relevant and with consent — An existing pregnancy
ruleOut.expectedFinding: A positive result changes investigation, medicine and counselling decisions.
ruleOut.targetCondition: An existing pregnancy
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Avoids treating the encounter as preconception when pregnancy has already begun.

ruleOut.testName: Immunisation and risk-based infection/genetic history
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Immunisation and risk-based infection/genetic history — Missing protection or a specific inherited/infectious risk
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Records and relevant family/exposure history select any indicated further tests.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Missing protection or a specific inherited/infectious risk
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Targets preventive care using current Saudi guidance instead of blanket testing.

pathophysiology.summary: Maternal health, chronic disease, medicines, nutrition, and environmental exposures can influence implantation, fetal development, and pregnancy outcomes. Preconception review provides an opportunity to optimise risks before conception. This topic is educational and should be interpreted alongside current local pathways and patient-specific assessment.
keyMechanisms: Maternal health, chronic disease, medicines, nutrition, and environmental exposures can influence implantation, fetal development, and pregnancy outcomes. Preconception review provides an opportunity to optimise risks before conception.
Clinical expression and progression vary with baseline risk, comorbidity, treatment exposure, and access to timely care.

title: Prelabour Rupture of Membranes
source_title: Gabbe's Obstetrics: Normal and Problem Pregnancies, 9th edition

redFlags: Fever, uterine tenderness, maternal/fetal tachycardia
Cord prolapse or abnormal presentation
Bleeding or suspected abruption
Reduced fetal movement or non-reassuring fetal status
symptoms: Evaluate the characteristic symptom pattern of Prelabour Rupture of Membranes, including onset, evolution, severity, associated symptoms, precipitating factors, complications, and relevant negative findings.
Clarify onset, progression, associated symptoms, baseline function, medicines and the patient’s own priorities.
Ask about relevant risk factors and context described in the case; document important negative findings rather than assuming their absence.
physicalSigns: Record observations and a focused examination directed to the organ system and competing diagnoses in this topic.
Assess functional change, comorbidity, hydration/perfusion where relevant, and baseline status.
Use serial reassessment when the condition or treatment can change over hours or days.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: History and testing help distinguish fluid source.
Speculum evaluation can clarify.
Contractions/cervical change may coexist.

ruleIn.testName: Sterile speculum examination and a validated membrane test when uncertain
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Sterile speculum examination and a validated membrane test when uncertain — Amniotic-fluid leakage
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Pooling or a positive validated test supports rupture in context; contamination and assay limitations may affect results.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Confirms the diagnosis while avoiding unnecessary repeated digital examination.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Ultrasound when indicated — Amniotic-fluid volume, presentation and growth
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Reduced fluid may support the context but cannot independently confirm or exclude rupture.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Assists pregnancy assessment and planning alongside examination and gestation.

ruleOut.testName: Maternal observations and fetal heart assessment
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Maternal observations and fetal heart assessment — Infection or fetal compromise
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Fever, maternal/fetal tachycardia or a concerning fetal pattern requires urgent obstetric reassessment.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Infection or fetal compromise
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Identifies complications that change the surveillance and delivery plan.

pathophysiology.summary: Membrane rupture before labour allows ascending infection and may precipitate birth; prematurity creates gestation-dependent neonatal risk. The balance between infection, labour, and neonatal maturity informs timing. This topic is educational and should be interpreted alongside current local pathways and patient-specific assessment.
keyMechanisms: Membrane rupture before labour allows ascending infection and may precipitate birth
prematurity creates gestation-dependent neonatal risk. The balance between infection, labour, and neonatal maturity informs timing.

title: Preterm Labour and Threatened Preterm Birth
source_title: Gabbe's Obstetrics: Normal and Problem Pregnancies, 9th edition

content.title: Preterm Labour and Threatened Preterm Birth

redFlags: Heavy bleeding, maternal instability, or suspected abruption
Fever, uterine tenderness, or foul fluid
Cord prolapse or fetal compromise
Advanced labour beyond local transfer capability
symptoms: Evaluate the characteristic symptom pattern of Preterm Labour and Threatened Preterm Birth, including onset, evolution, severity, associated symptoms, precipitating factors, complications, and relevant negative findings.
Clarify onset, progression, associated symptoms, baseline function, medicines and the patient’s own priorities.
Ask about relevant risk factors and context described in the case; document important negative findings rather than assuming their absence.
physicalSigns: Record observations and a focused examination directed to the organ system and competing diagnoses in this topic.
Assess functional change, comorbidity, hydration/perfusion where relevant, and baseline status.
Use serial reassessment when the condition or treatment can change over hours or days.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: No progressive cervical change and symptoms may settle.
Can cause uterine irritability and requires assessment.
Pain, bleeding, uterine tone, or fetal concern changes urgency.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Contraction, cervical and gestation assessment — Labour-associated cervical change before term
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Contractions with progressive cervical change support labour; isolated contractions are insufficient.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Determines whether urgent preterm-birth planning is needed.

ruleIn.testName: Transvaginal cervical length or a validated prediction test when indicated
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Transvaginal cervical length or a validated prediction test when indicated — Risk of imminent preterm birth
ruleIn.expectedFinding: A short cervix or test result is interpreted within the locally adopted gestation-specific algorithm.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Refines risk when clinical diagnosis is uncertain; eligibility and interpretation follow the obstetric pathway.

ruleOut.testName: Maternal observations, urine testing and membrane assessment when indicated
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Maternal observations, urine testing and membrane assessment when indicated — Infection or membrane rupture contributing to symptoms
ruleOut.expectedFinding: An infectious finding or fluid leakage directs a separate treatment pathway.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Infection or membrane rupture contributing to symptoms
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Detects causes and complications that change management and the appropriateness of examination/testing.

pathophysiology.summary: Preterm labour involves uterine activity with cervical remodelling before term and may arise spontaneously or from infection, placental disease, or maternal/fetal indication. Neonatal risk depends strongly on gestational age and available care. This topic is educational and should be interpreted alongside current local pathways and patient-specific assessment.
keyMechanisms: Preterm labour involves uterine activity with cervical remodelling before term and may arise spontaneously or from infection, placental disease, or maternal/fetal indication. Neonatal risk depends strongly on gestational age and available care.
Clinical expression and progression vary with baseline risk, comorbidity, treatment exposure, and access to timely care.

title: Sepsis
source_title: MOH-context sepsis pathway synthesis for local governance review

content.title: Sepsis
content.specialty: Emergency Medicine, Internal Medicine and Critical Care

redFlags: Persistent hypotension or evidence of hypoperfusion after initial fluid resuscitation
New altered consciousness, rapidly increasing oxygen need or respiratory failure
Lactate elevation with clinical deterioration or oliguria
Purpura, necrotising soft-tissue features, meningism or a source needing immediate surgical control
symptoms: Fever, rigors or feeling unusually cold
New confusion, profound weakness or reduced urine output
Breathlessness, cough, dysuria, abdominal pain or another focal infection symptom
Rapid deterioration in a patient with recent infection, procedure or immunosuppression
physicalSigns: Altered mental status
Tachypnoea, hypoxaemia or increased work of breathing
Hypotension, prolonged capillary refill, mottling or cool peripheries
Oliguria, tachycardia or abnormal temperature

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Ischaemic symptoms, pulmonary congestion, elevated jugular venous pressure or cardiac imaging suggesting pump failure.
History of bleeding or fluid loss without a convincing infectious focus; response depends on correction of the volume deficit.
Abrupt onset after exposure with skin or mucosal findings, bronchospasm or gastrointestinal symptoms.
Sudden dyspnoea or pleuritic pain, thromboembolic risk and right-heart strain without a clear infection syndrome.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Serum lactate with repeat trend — Tissue hypoperfusion
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Elevation or failure to clear in a clinically deteriorating patient.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Supports severity assessment and response monitoring but must be interpreted with the whole clinical picture.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Blood cultures and source-directed microbiology — Causative infection
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Growth or molecular detection of a plausible pathogen from blood or the suspected source.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Enables antimicrobial narrowing and source-directed care; obtain before antibiotics only when this does not cause harmful delay.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Organ-function panel — Sepsis-associated organ dysfunction
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Acute kidney, liver, coagulation, haematological or gas-exchange abnormality.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Defines severity, guides support and provides a baseline for trends.

ruleOut.testName: Electrocardiogram and cardiac biomarkers when indicated
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Electrocardiogram and cardiac biomarkers when indicated — Acute coronary syndrome or primary cardiac shock
ruleOut.expectedFinding: No primary ischaemic pattern explaining the haemodynamic state.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Acute coronary syndrome or primary cardiac shock
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Cardiac disease can mimic or coexist with sepsis and changes fluid and vasopressor decisions.

ruleOut.testName: Source-directed imaging
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Source-directed imaging — Non-infectious mimic or drainable focus
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Imaging identifies or excludes pneumonia, obstruction, perforation, abscess or another urgent source.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Non-infectious mimic or drainable focus
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Confirms anatomy and determines whether procedural source control is required.

pathophysiology.summary: Sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection. Endothelial injury, vasodilation, capillary leak, microvascular thrombosis and cellular metabolic dysfunction can impair tissue oxygen delivery and progress to shock and multiorgan failure.
keyMechanisms: An uncontrolled inflammatory and immune response disrupts endothelial integrity and vascular tone.
Relative and absolute hypovolaemia reduce effective circulating volume.
Microcirculatory dysfunction and coagulation activation impair organ perfusion.
Myocardial depression and cellular oxygen-utilisation defects can persist despite apparently corrected blood pressure.

clinicalManagement.title: Recognise sepsis and grade urgency
actions: Assess airway, breathing, circulation, mental status, perfusion and urine output.
Record observations and identify high-risk organ dysfunction without relying on a single screening score.
Activate senior and critical-care escalation for shock or rapidly worsening physiology.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Immediately

clinicalManagement.title: Obtain time-critical diagnostics
actions: Measure lactate and obtain blood count, renal, liver, coagulation and glucose studies.
Take blood cultures and appropriate source specimens before antimicrobials when this can be done promptly.
Use targeted imaging to locate infection and source-control needs.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: As early as possible without delaying treatment

clinicalManagement.title: Start infection and perfusion treatment
actions: Administer empiric intravenous antimicrobials selected for the suspected source, local resistance patterns, allergies and recent exposure.
Give balanced crystalloid in reassessed aliquots when hypoperfusion is present, accounting for cardiac or renal risk.
Provide oxygen and organ support according to measured need.
Start vasopressor support in a monitored setting under critical-care oversight.
Use dynamic reassessment to avoid both under-resuscitation and fluid overload.
branches.condition: Hypotension persists despite appropriate initial fluid

clinicalManagement.timeframe: Immediately for shock or high-likelihood sepsis

clinicalManagement.title: Achieve source control
actions: Request surgical, interventional radiology or specialty review for drainage, debridement or device removal.
Do not defer an urgent source-control procedure solely to complete non-essential tests.
Document the source-control decision and planned timing.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Urgently once the source is identified

clinicalManagement.title: Reassess and de-escalate
actions: Trend haemodynamics, lactate, urine output, oxygen need and organ function.
Review microbiology and narrow, change or stop antimicrobials when evidence supports it.
Reconsider the diagnosis and seek additional source control if improvement is inadequate.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Continuously, with formal review after initial resuscitation

nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Arrange source-appropriate clinical review and results follow-up, reconcile antimicrobials and other medicines, screen for post-sepsis functional or psychological problems, and escalate persistent fatigue, breathlessness, cognitive change or recurrent fever.
mdtReferrals: Critical care for shock, respiratory failure or escalating organ support
Source-specific surgical or procedural team
Microbiology or infectious diseases for complex infection or antimicrobial stewardship
Physiotherapy, dietetics and rehabilitation after prolonged or severe illness
lifestyleAndDiet: Support nutrition, hydration and mobilisation during recovery according to swallowing and organ-function assessment.
Review indicated vaccination and infection-prevention measures after the acute episode.
Address smoking and other modifiable infection risks when clinically stable.
patientEducation: Explain the suspected source, organ effects and why treatment and monitoring are time critical.
On recovery, provide signs of recurrent infection or deterioration that require urgent assessment.
Discuss antimicrobial purpose, planned review and potential adverse effects.
dischargeCriteria: Infection source and treatment plan are established with stable physiology.
Organ dysfunction has resolved or has a safe documented outpatient plan.
Oral therapy, monitoring, follow-up and explicit return precautions are feasible and understood.

title: Severe Hypoglycaemia
source_title: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd edition

redFlags: Seizure, coma, or airway compromise
Recurrent low glucose after initial response
Persistent focal deficit after glucose correction
Suspected overdose, trauma, or inability to maintain glucose safely
symptoms: Evaluate the characteristic symptom pattern of Severe Hypoglycaemia, including onset, evolution, severity, associated symptoms, precipitating factors, complications, and relevant negative findings.
Clarify onset, progression, associated symptoms, baseline function, medicines and the patient’s own priorities.
Ask about relevant risk factors and context described in the case; document important negative findings rather than assuming their absence.
physicalSigns: Record observations and a focused examination directed to the organ system and competing diagnoses in this topic.
Assess functional change, comorbidity, hydration/perfusion where relevant, and baseline status.
Use serial reassessment when the condition or treatment can change over hours or days.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Persistent focal signs after euglycaemia need urgent neurological work-up.
Consider if events persist after correction or history supports it.
Consider when context or recovery is atypical.

ruleIn.testName: Immediate bedside glucose with repeat measurement
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Immediate bedside glucose with repeat measurement — Low glucose and response to correction
ruleIn.expectedFinding: A low result supports hypoglycaemia; a repeat measurement checks recovery or recurrence.
ruleIn.targetCondition: Low glucose and response to correction
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Confirms the reversible emergency and monitors treatment without delaying immediate care.

ruleOut.testName: Medication, intake and renal/hepatic assessment
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Medication, intake and renal/hepatic assessment — Drug accumulation, missed intake or impaired glucose regulation
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Recent insulin/sulfonylurea exposure, poor intake or organ dysfunction may explain prolonged or recurrent episodes.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Drug accumulation, missed intake or impaired glucose regulation
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Identifies the trigger and determines monitoring needs and recurrence prevention.

ruleOut.testName: Specialist-directed critical-sample testing for unexplained recurrent episodes
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Specialist-directed critical-sample testing for unexplained recurrent episodes — Endogenous or exogenous hyperinsulinaemia and other causes
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Selected glucose, insulin-related and exposure assays require interpretation at the time of a documented episode.

title: Tobacco and Nicotine Cessation

Severe mood symptoms or suicidality
Possible acute nicotine poisoning
Concurrent substance use or unstable psychiatric illness
symptoms: Evaluate the characteristic symptom pattern of Tobacco and Nicotine Cessation, including onset, evolution, severity, associated symptoms, precipitating factors, complications, and relevant negative findings.
Clarify onset, progression, associated symptoms, baseline function, medicines and the patient’s own priorities.
Ask about relevant risk factors and context described in the case; document important negative findings rather than assuming their absence.
physicalSigns: Record observations and a focused examination directed to the organ system and competing diagnoses in this topic.
Assess functional change, comorbidity, hydration/perfusion where relevant, and baseline status.
Use serial reassessment when the condition or treatment can change over hours or days.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Clarify all inhaled substances and goals.
Assess symptoms and product combination.
Treat symptoms while supporting cessation.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Structured tobacco-use and dependence assessment — Nicotine dependence and withdrawal risk
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Product use, frequency, time to first use and prior withdrawal define the dependence pattern.

ruleOut.testName: Pregnancy, mental-health and medication review
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Pregnancy, mental-health and medication review — Factors affecting cessation treatment safety and follow-up

title: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus Longitudinal Care
source_title: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd edition

redFlags: Ketosis or severe dehydration
Rapid unexplained weight loss or new severe hyperglycaemia
Foot ulcer with infection/ischaemia
Acute visual change or pregnancy with poor control
symptoms: Evaluate the characteristic symptom pattern of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus Longitudinal Care, including onset, evolution, severity, associated symptoms, precipitating factors, complications, and relevant negative findings.
Clarify onset, progression, associated symptoms, baseline function, medicines and the patient’s own priorities.
Ask about relevant risk factors and context described in the case; document important negative findings rather than assuming their absence.
physicalSigns: Record observations and a focused examination directed to the organ system and competing diagnoses in this topic.
Assess functional change, comorbidity, hydration/perfusion where relevant, and baseline status.
Use serial reassessment when the condition or treatment can change over hours or days.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Ketosis, rapid insulin need, or autoimmune history may prompt reclassification.
Review glucocorticoids and other contributing drugs.
Pancreatic or endocrine context may warrant evaluation.

ruleIn.testName: HbA1c or an appropriate glucose-based measure
ruleIn.modalityTarget: HbA1c or an appropriate glucose-based measure — Current glycaemic control
ruleIn.expectedFinding: The result shows overall control in context; use glucose-based measures when HbA1c is unreliable.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Guides shared treatment review while considering hypoglycaemia, frailty and individual goals.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Creatinine/eGFR and urine albumin-creatinine ratio — Reduced filtration or albuminuria
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Persistent abnormalities identify diabetic or other kidney disease and modify risk.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Detects renal complications and informs medication safety and monitoring.

ruleOut.testName: Retinal assessment and foot-risk examination
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Retinal assessment and foot-risk examination — Retinopathy, neuropathy, ischaemia or ulceration
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Retinal abnormalities, reduced protective sensation or abnormal pulses require tracked follow-up.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Retinopathy, neuropathy, ischaemia or ulceration
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Finds complications early and directs preventive or urgent specialist care.

ruleOut.testName: Lipid profile and cardiovascular assessment
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Lipid profile and cardiovascular assessment — Atherogenic risk and established vascular disease
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Lipid abnormalities and vascular history influence prevention priorities.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Atherogenic risk and established vascular disease
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Addresses cardiovascular risk alongside glucose control under the current Saudi diabetes pathway.

pathophysiology.summary: Insulin resistance and progressive beta-cell dysfunction produce chronic hyperglycaemia. Vascular, renal, retinal, neural, and metabolic complications accrue over time, with risk shaped by blood pressure, lipids, kidney status, and social determinants. This topic is educational and should be interpreted alongside current local pathways and patient-specific assessment.
keyMechanisms: Insulin resistance and progressive beta-cell dysfunction produce chronic hyperglycaemia. Vascular, renal, retinal, neural, and metabolic complications accrue over time, with risk shaped by blood pressure, lipids, kidney status, and social determinants.
Clinical expression and progression vary with baseline risk, comorbidity, treatment exposure, and access to timely care.

title: Venous Thromboembolism in Pregnancy and Postpartum
source_title: Gabbe's Obstetrics: Normal and Problem Pregnancies, 9th edition

content.title: Venous Thromboembolism in Pregnancy and Postpartum

redFlags: Syncope, hypoxaemia, shock, or severe chest pain
Rapidly progressive swelling or suspected phlegmasia
Major bleeding or thrombocytopenia
Labour or planned neuraxial procedure while anticoagulated
symptoms: Evaluate the characteristic symptom pattern of Venous Thromboembolism in Pregnancy and Postpartum, including onset, evolution, severity, associated symptoms, precipitating factors, complications, and relevant negative findings.
Clarify onset, progression, associated symptoms, baseline function, medicines and the patient’s own priorities.
Ask about relevant risk factors and context described in the case; document important negative findings rather than assuming their absence.
physicalSigns: Record observations and a focused examination directed to the organ system and competing diagnoses in this topic.
Assess functional change, comorbidity, hydration/perfusion where relevant, and baseline status.
Use serial reassessment when the condition or treatment can change over hours or days.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Usually bilateral and gradual but does not exclude DVT.
Alternative causes of chest symptoms.
Peripartum collapse is distinct and immediately critical.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Compression ultrasound for suspected DVT — Venous thrombosis
ruleIn.expectedFinding: A non-compressible vein supports DVT; persistent suspicion after a negative study requires the pregnancy-specific follow-up pathway.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Provides first-line objective assessment of symptomatic leg-vein thrombosis.

ruleIn.testName: Pregnancy-adapted PE assessment and specialist-selected chest imaging
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Pregnancy-adapted PE assessment and specialist-selected chest imaging — Pulmonary embolism
ruleIn.expectedFinding: The selected V/Q or CT pulmonary angiographic study is interpreted within the pregnancy diagnostic pathway.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Confirms or excludes PE with an appropriate balance of clinical risk, radiation and contrast considerations.

ruleOut.testName: Full blood count, creatinine and bleeding assessment
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Full blood count, creatinine and bleeding assessment — Anaemia, thrombocytopenia, renal impairment or bleeding risk
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Abnormal platelets/haemoglobin or renal function may change anticoagulation and monitoring.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Anaemia, thrombocytopenia, renal impairment or bleeding risk
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Establishes treatment safety without delaying urgent care for a suspected high-risk thromboembolic event.

pathophysiology.summary: Pregnancy increases venous stasis and coagulation tendency while reducing fibrinolysis; risk remains elevated postpartum. Thromboembolism threatens maternal oxygenation and requires coordinated diagnostic and anticoagulation planning. This topic is educational and should be interpreted alongside current local pathways and patient-specific assessment.
keyMechanisms: Pregnancy increases venous stasis and coagulation tendency while reducing fibrinolysis
risk remains elevated postpartum. Thromboembolism threatens maternal oxygenation and requires coordinated diagnostic and anticoagulation planning.
